questions.text: What is the single biggest thing preventing your ecommerce from growing right now?

teach.why: The whole offer is sized against one problem statement. It decides whether this is a storefront build, a replatform, an operations fix or a growth programme, and it is the line the closing document and the backlog are judged against.

questions.text: How long has this been a problem, and what have you already tried to fix it?

teach.why: Tells you whether the problem is platform-shaped or organisational. A client who has already bought three apps for this has a diagnosis problem, not a build problem. It also shows which solutions have been tried and rejected.

questions.text: If we solved only one thing in this engagement, what would have the highest business impact?

teach.why: Forces one priority before scope is negotiated. It sets phase one of the backlog and gives you the line to defend when items are added later.

questions.text: What is your current monthly ecommerce revenue (range and currency)?

teach.why: The revenue band sizes the offer and sanity-checks plan and budget. Card rates and transaction fees fall as the plan rises, so volume decides whether a higher plan pays for itself.
teach.limits: Prices and card rates are shown in local currency and differ by region — re-check Shopify's pricing page for the client's own market before quoting any number.

questions.text: What is your current conversion rate (%)?

teach.why: The baseline conversion rate tells you whether the brief is a build or an optimisation programme, and gives the KPI the project will be measured on. A very low rate points at checkout, catalogue and performance work rather than a new theme.

questions.text: Which product categories, markets or customer segments under-perform?

teach.why: Names where the money is being lost. Under-performing countries pull in Markets scope — currency, pricing, language, domains; under-performing categories usually point at merchandising, search and product data instead.

questions.text: Is the main bottleneck acquisition (traffic), conversion (traffic doesn't buy) or retention (customers don't return)?

teach.why: This routes the whole solution. Acquisition points at sales channels, SEO and new markets; conversion at theme, search and checkout; retention at customer accounts, subscriptions and messaging. Each gives a different backlog and a different app shortlist.

questions.text: What share of revenue comes from each channel today (online store, retail stores, marketplaces, social commerce, wholesale / B2B, other)?
questions.help: Tells us whether retail, B2B and marketplace scope are in play.

teach.why: Channel mix shows how much of the work sits outside the online store. Retail brings POS and inventory locations, wholesale brings B2B scope, marketplaces and social bring extra sales channels — each is separate configuration and separate backlog.

questions.text: How many orders per month do you expect in the first year?
questions.help: Returns, tracking and fraud apps are priced by order volume.

teach.why: Order volume drives recurring cost more than build cost: returns, tracking, fraud and review apps are priced by order band. It also sizes the order-history migration and the fulfilment set-up.
teach.limits: On a trial or development store the orderCreate mutation is capped at five new orders per minute, so a full-volume order import cannot be rehearsed there.

questions.text: What manual work does your team do today that the platform should automate, and which processes break most often?

teach.why: Manual work is where a Shopify project earns its return. Each item becomes a Flow automation, an integration, an app or an admin change — this is the main source of backlog items outside the storefront.

questions.text: How many hours per week does the team spend on workarounds?

teach.why: Puts a number on the operational case, so automation scope can be argued on cost rather than opinion. Feeds the business case and the offer, not the architecture.

questions.text: What does success look like in 12 months (revenue, new markets, channels, customer volume)?

teach.why: Twelve-month goals decide what must be designed for now rather than later: new countries mean Markets, new channels mean sales channels, volume means plan and API headroom. It separates launch scope from roadmap.

questions.text: Which KPIs will measure success? For each: metric, today's baseline, target, horizon in months.

teach.why: Baselines and targets give the project measurable acceptance. Without today's number no post-launch claim can be made. It also tells you which analytics and tracking must be live at launch, not after it.

questions.text: What triggered this engagement — why Shopify, and why now?

teach.why: The trigger tells you who is really driving and what the deadline is — a contract renewal, a failed replatform, a funding round. It sets urgency, the decision-maker, and how much of the current set-up is genuinely open to change.

questions.text: If you are moving from another platform, what must not be lost in the transition?

teach.why: The must-not-be-lost list is the migration risk register: URLs and search ranking, order history, customer accounts, integrations, reviews. Each item is either inside Shopify's import path or a separate, costed workstream.
teach.limits: Customer passwords cannot be migrated by CSV, because they are encrypted outside Shopify; customers are invited to set a new password, or sign in with an emailed 6-digit code. Reviews cannot be exported from Squarespace. Indexing of new pages can take 48 to 72 hours, and traffic recovery longer.

questions.text: What are you most unhappy with in the current store or set-up?

teach.why: Frustrations name what the client will judge the new store against on day one. They convert directly into backlog items and into the design brief — and sometimes show the platform was never the problem.

questions.text: Which platform are you migrating from (or none — greenfield)?
questions.help: Shopify's Store Migration app imports products and customers from some platforms (e.g. WooCommerce, Wix, Square); other platforms use a migration app or the API.

teach.why: Decides the migration route and its cost. Shopify's own Store Migration app covers a documented list of source platforms, products and customers only; anything else, and all order history, needs a migration app or API work. It triggers the Migration scope modifier.

options.option: Shopify Store Migration app (CSV, documented source platforms)
options.pros: First-party, no licence cost, per-item error report.
options.cons: Products and customers only — no order history, no prices by location, three product options maximum.

options.pros: Moves products, customers and order history together with no engineering build.
options.cons: App licence and third-party support; Shopify's partner guidance frames this route for Plus clients.

options.pros: Full control of mapping for non-standard source data and large volumes.
options.cons: Build and test effort; 100 MB JSONL and 24-hour operation limits; dev-store order rate cap blocks rehearsal.

teach.limits: The Store Migration app documents Amazon, Clover, Etsy, eBay, GoDaddy, Lightspeed, Square, Squarespace, Wix and WooCommerce as sources, and imports products and customers, not historical orders. Products with more than three options lose their options on import; prices by location are not supported. Import order is products, then customers, then orders. URL redirects are capped at 100,000, or 20,000,000 on Plus. Turn off new-order notifications before importing orders, or every imported order emails staff.

questions.text: What is the approximate budget envelope for this project (range and currency)?

teach.why: The budget band picks the offer size and decides how much can be native configuration rather than custom build. It also surfaces the mismatch case early, where the requirements need a plan or a build the envelope will not carry.

questions.text: Is the priority to minimise upfront cost (apps and configuration), to own the solution (custom build), or a balance?

teach.why: Sets the build philosophy. Apps and configuration launch faster and cost monthly; a custom build costs more upfront and is owned outright. It changes the architecture, the app shortlist and the store's running cost.

options.pros: Fastest to launch, lowest upfront cost, vendor maintains the functionality.
options.cons: Permanent monthly subscriptions, limited control, and a vendor's roadmap decides what changes.

options.pros: Exactly the required behaviour, owned by the client, no per-app subscription.
options.cons: Higher upfront cost and an ongoing maintenance commitment; a Shopify Function inside a custom app requires Plus.

teach.limits: Public App Store apps containing Shopify Functions install on any plan; Functions inside a custom app built for one merchant require Plus.

questions.text: Is there a monthly ceiling for app subscriptions?
questions.help: Many needs are covered by Shopify's own apps (e.g. Subscriptions, Bundles, Search & Discovery, Translate & Adapt, Flow, Messaging). We check those first.

teach.why: App subscriptions are a permanent line in the client's P&L, so a stated ceiling constrains the shortlist. Check Shopify's own apps first — Subscriptions, Bundles, Search & Discovery, Translate & Adapt, Flow, Messaging — before proposing paid third parties.

questions.text: Trading name and legal entity name (if different).

teach.why: The legal entity is what the Shopify account, the bank account and the store policies are held in; the trading name is what customers see. Capturing both now stops a mismatch appearing during payments verification.
teach.limits: Shopify Payments requires a business entity and a bank account in an eligible region, and each supported country has its own bank account and business verification requirements.

questions.text: Country of incorporation / headquarters.

teach.why: The country of incorporation sets the store's primary country, which decides payment provider availability, payout currency, tax set-up and the base market everything else is configured around.
teach.limits: Shopify Payments is available only in supported countries and regions; confirm the client's entity country on Shopify's supported-countries index before assuming it is an option. The currency conversion fee is based on the store's primary country.

questions.text: Industry and product vertical.

teach.why: The vertical decides catalogue complexity, content needs and, critically, legal exposure. Regulated categories — pharma, alcohol, firearms, age-restricted goods, financial products, medical devices — trigger a STOP for legal and compliance review before any scope is committed.

questions.text: Is the business direct-to-consumer, B2B, or hybrid?
questions.help: B2B or hybrid brings the B2B and wholesale questions (§ 6.2).

teach.why: Decides whether wholesale scope is in play at all. B2B or hybrid opens the § 6.2 questions and the B2B scope modifier: companies, company locations, catalogs, payment terms and PO numbers — a different data model from D2C, not a discount setting.

options.option: Blended store — one store serving D2C and B2B
options.pros: One catalogue, one admin, one theme to maintain; B2B pricing is layered on with catalogs.
options.cons: Every storefront and checkout decision must work for both audiences, and B2B checkout restrictions apply.

options.option: Dedicated B2B store, separate from D2C
options.pros: Clean separation of experience, pricing and operations; nothing D2C constrains the trade site.
options.cons: A second store to build, run and keep in sync; expansion stores are a Plus feature.

teach.limits: Native B2B runs on every plan from Basic: companies, locations, net terms, PO numbers, quantity rules and price breaks. Basic, Grow and Advanced allow up to 3 active catalogs across all B2B markets and require new Shopify Markets; unlimited catalogs, catalogs assigned to a company or location, deposits and partial payments are Plus. B2B checkout does not support accelerated payments (Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Amazon Pay), subscriptions or legacy customer accounts.

questions.text: Current website URL.

teach.why: The current site is the fastest evidence you get: catalogue size, option complexity, content volume, current platform and the integrations visible from outside. It also grounds the redirect and SEO workstream if this is a replatform.

questions.text: Do you sell through more than one legal entity (e.g. one per country or region)? List them.
questions.help: Several selling entities in one store, or one store per entity, changes the store set-up.

native.plan_note: Needs Shopify Payments and the new Markets; otherwise expansion stores

teach.why: Decides the store topology. Several selling entities in one store means one admin with per-market entities; one store per entity means several stores to build and run. It changes tax, payouts, invoicing and the plan, and it feeds the plan-gate STOP.

options.option: One store, several business entities per market
options.pros: One catalogue, one admin and one theme, with per-market entity, payouts and tax.
options.cons: Plus only, and requires Shopify Payments plus the new Markets.

options.pros: Hard separation of data, staff, finance and local operations.
options.cons: Plus only; every catalogue, theme and app change has to be repeated across stores.

teach.limits: Assigning separate business entities to markets is Plus only, and needs Shopify Payments and the new Markets; otherwise the route is expansion stores, which are also Plus (one main store plus nine expansion stores on the contract).

questions.text: Where will you sell at launch?
questions.help: Online store, Shopify POS, Shop app, marketplaces, social channels, B2B, headless or app front ends, AI shopping agents.

native.feature: Sales channels (Online Store, POS, Shop, Marketplace Connect, Facebook & Instagram, Google & YouTube, TikTok)

teach.why: Launch channels decide how much is built beyond the online store. Each channel is its own set-up and its own backlog: POS, Shop, Marketplace Connect, Facebook and Instagram, Google and YouTube, TikTok, or a headless front end on the Storefront API.

options.option: Shopify's online store (Liquid theme) as the front end
options.pros: Fastest to launch, editable by the client, works with theme apps and the standard checkout.
options.cons: Front-end freedom is bounded by the theme and section model.

options.option: Headless front end on the Storefront API
options.pros: Full control of the experience and of front-end technology choices.
options.cons: A build and a hosting commitment; merchandising by theme editor is lost unless replaced.

teach.limits: The standard sales channels and the headless channel are available from Basic. Agentic storefronts (ChatGPT, Google AI Mode and Gemini, Copilot, Meta) are active by default for eligible stores, so 'AI shopping agents' is usually a decision about what to leave on, not a build.

questions.text: Is there an existing Shopify store?

teach.why: Decides the starting point: configure and improve what exists, or build a new store and migrate onto it. It changes the delivery approach, the risk profile and whether an audit of the current store is part of the engagement.

options.pros: Keeps order and customer history, apps, domains and SEO in place; no data migration.
options.cons: Inherits the existing theme, app estate and any deprecated features, and changes are made on a live, trading store.

options.option: Build a new store and migrate
options.pros: Clean architecture and data model, and a safe place to build away from live trade.
options.cons: A migration and cutover to plan and pay for, with redirect and SEO risk at launch.

questions.text: Existing store URL, current Shopify plan and current theme.

teach.why: The current plan and theme set the baseline: which features the client already has, whether the theme is a supported Online Store 2.0 theme or a customised legacy one, and how much of the existing build can be carried forward.

questions.text: Which Shopify plan will the new store run on (if already decided)?
questions.help: We recommend the plan once the requirements are known.

native.plan_note: The minimum plan is derived from the requirements (exit rule 11.1)

teach.why: The plan is the hardest constraint in a Shopify project — several features are plan-gated, not build-gated. Recommend it from the requirements, then check the client's assumption against it; a mismatch is a STOP, not a detail.
teach.limits: Documented gates that most often decide the plan: staff users (Basic 0, Grow 5, Advanced 15, Plus unlimited); more than 10 inventory locations, checkout UI extensions on the information, shipping or payment steps, the Checkout Branding API, expansion stores, business entities per market, more than 20 published languages, combined listings and Functions in a custom app are Plus; per-market theme customisation, carrier-calculated rates and multi-currency payouts start at Advanced.

questions.text: Which apps are installed today, what do they do, and which must stay?

teach.why: The installed app list is both a cost line and a requirements document — each app is a job the store does today. Which must stay decides what the new build has to keep working, and which can be replaced by a native feature.

questions.text: Existing store audit: which retired or deprecated Shopify features does it still use?
questions.help: Shopify Scripts stopped running on 2026-06-30; checkout.liquid and additional scripts are retired; online store script tags stop on 2027-03-01; legacy customer accounts are deprecated; Stocky is retired; the Geolocation app is retired.

native.plan_note: Scripts stopped running 2026-06-30

native.feature: Inventory purchase orders and transfers (Stocky retired 2026-08-31)

teach.why: Retired and deprecated features are silent breakage: logic that has already stopped running, or will. Any hit becomes its own workstream — Scripts to Functions, script tags to theme app extensions, legacy to current customer accounts — flagged, not absorbed into theme work.

options.option: Fix the deprecations first, as their own workstream
options.pros: Removes the breakage risk before new work is built on top of it.
options.cons: Spends budget on parity rather than on anything the client can see.

options.option: Fold the replacements into the new build
options.pros: One design pass, one test cycle, no work done twice.
options.cons: Anything already retired stays broken until the new build ships.

teach.limits: Shopify Scripts stopped running on 2026-06-30; checkout.liquid and additional scripts are retired; online store script tags stop on 2027-03-01; legacy customer accounts were deprecated on 2026-02-26; Stocky was retired on 2026-08-31, replaced by inventory purchase orders and transfers; the Geolocation app is retired.

questions.text: How many people need their own Shopify admin login after go-live?
questions.help: Collaborator accounts and POS-only staff are not counted.

native.plan_note: Basic 0, Grow 5, Advanced 15, Plus unlimited; collaborators and POS-only staff not counted

teach.why: Named admin users are a plan gate, not a licence add-on. The headcount can move the store up a plan on its own, so it has to be counted before the plan is quoted.
teach.limits: Basic 0 staff accounts, Grow 5, Advanced 15, Plus unlimited. Collaborator accounts (agency access) and POS-only staff are not counted against the limit.

questions.text: How would you describe the brand's positioning: value, mid-market, premium, luxury or enterprise?
questions.help: Positioning shapes the design depth and the solution approach.

teach.why: Positioning sets the design depth and the solution approach. Luxury and enterprise positioning triggers the L offer: bespoke design, more front-end build and a longer review cycle, rather than a configured theme.

questions.text: Is the brand identity finalised (logo, colour palette, typography)?

teach.why: An unfinished identity is a schedule risk, not a design preference. If logo, palette and type are still moving, theme and design work either waits or is built twice — decide which, and price it.

options.option: Start the build on the current identity
options.pros: Keeps the delivery dates; tokens and theme settings absorb later colour and type changes.
options.cons: Anything structural that changes with the identity is rework.

options.option: Wait for the identity to be signed off
options.pros: One design pass, no rework, cleaner approvals.
options.cons: Idle delivery time and a launch date that depends on someone outside the project.

questions.text: In which formats are brand assets available (SVG, PNG, Figma, guidelines PDF)?

teach.why: Asset formats decide how much production work sits in the design phase. Vector logos and a Figma file feed straight into the theme; a guidelines PDF and print-resolution assets mean redrawing and re-exporting before anything reaches the store.

questions.text: Are there strict brand guidelines that must be followed?

teach.why: Strict guidelines mean a review and approval cycle on every screen, and less freedom to use the theme's own components. That is delivery time and effort, and it belongs in the estimate rather than in a surprise later.

questions.text: What differentiates the brand — price, quality, exclusivity, community, sustainability?

teach.why: Differentiators tell you what the storefront actually has to prove — sustainability needs product data and content, exclusivity needs gated or limited-release mechanics, community needs reviews and accounts. Each becomes concrete backlog, not brand language.

questions.text: Who are your top three online competitors?

teach.why: Competitors set the client's expectation of normal. They tell you which features will be asked for mid-project, and give a concrete reference for the design and UX conversation instead of adjectives.

questions.text: Which stores (competitor or not) have a UX you want to reference?

teach.why: UX references convert taste into specifics — navigation, product page, cart and checkout behaviour. Use them to agree scope on the front end before design starts, and to identify which behaviours need an app or custom work.

questions.text: How many active SKUs are in the catalogue (approximate)?

teach.why: Catalogue size sets the build and migration effort and feeds the SKU complexity scope gate: 500 SKUs or more, combined with multiple variant options, custom attributes or bundles, adds the +SKU modifier to the offer.

questions.text: What is the maximum number of variant options on a product (e.g. size, colour, material = 3)?
questions.help: Shopify allows up to 3 options per product; more options need a different product model.

native.plan_note: Up to 60 child products

teach.why: Shopify models a product with at most three options (for example size, colour, material). A fourth option means the product model has to change, so this answer decides the data model before anything is priced or migrated.
teach.limits: Up to 3 options per product. Beyond that, Shopify documents combined listings (Plus only, up to 60 child products), a product options app for choices that are not stock, or splitting the product. During a CSV or migration-app import, options past the third are not imported. Exit rule 11.5 flags this for a product model review.

questions.text: What is the maximum number of variants on a single product?
questions.help: Shopify allows up to 2,048 variants per product.

native.plan_note: Apps must use the current GraphQL product APIs above 100 variants

teach.why: The largest product in the catalogue tells you whether the variant ceiling is in play. A product over the limit has to be split or restructured, which changes SKUs, URLs and the import plan, so it is found now rather than at data load.
teach.limits: Up to 2,048 variants per product. Above 100 variants, apps must use the current GraphQL product APIs, which matters for any integration or bulk update tooling.

questions.text: Are variants such as colours managed as separate products (own SKUs, images, URLs) that should appear as one product on the storefront?
questions.help: This is what Shopify calls combined listings.

teach.why: Shopify calls this a combined listing: separate products, each with its own SKUs, images and URL, shown to shoppers as one product. It is a Plus-only app, so a yes here can force the plan up. Exit rule 11.1 triggers.

options.pros: Each colour keeps its own SKU, images and URL while the storefront shows one product.
options.cons: Requires the Plus plan, so the whole engagement carries the higher plan cost.

options.option: One product with colour as a variant option
options.pros: Works from Basic, within the three-option and 2,048-variant limits.
options.cons: Colours lose their own product URL, and SEO and paid feeds built on the per-colour URLs have to be reworked.

teach.limits: The Combined Listings app is available only on Plus and enterprise plans, with up to 60 child products per listing.

questions.text: Which product types exist in the catalogue?
questions.help: Shopify Bundles creates fixed bundles and multipacks; mix-and-match bundles need an app.

teach.why: Product types decide what is native and what needs an app. Fixed bundles, multipacks, subscriptions and gift cards are native from Basic; mix-and-match bundles and pre-orders need apps. It also feeds the SKU complexity gate.
teach.limits: Shopify Bundles covers fixed bundles and multipacks. Mix-and-match bundles need an app. Pre-orders always need an app.

questions.text: Will subscriptions run on Shopify Subscriptions (Shopify's app) or a third-party subscription app? Name the app if known.
questions.help: Shopify Subscriptions: customers skip, pause and cancel in their account; not with bundles or B2B.

native.plan_note: Not with bundles, B2B or draft orders; limited gateways

teach.why: Shopify's own Subscriptions app is free and lets customers skip, pause and cancel from their account, but it does not work with bundles, B2B or draft orders and supports a limited set of gateways. Those exclusions decide whether a paid app enters the cost model.

options.pros: First-party, no licence fee, self-service management in the customer account.
options.cons: Ruled out by bundles, B2B or an unsupported gateway.

options.pros: Covers the cases Shopify's app excludes and richer subscriber management.
options.cons: Monthly licence, often a revenue share, and a second system holding subscriber and payment data.

teach.limits: Shopify Subscriptions is not compatible with bundles, B2B or draft orders, and supports limited payment gateways.

questions.text: If you sell bundles: what must they do?
questions.help: Shopify Bundles: up to 30 components; not with subscriptions or pre-orders; no nested bundles.

native.plan_note: Up to 30 components; not with subscriptions or pre-orders

teach.why: The detail of what a bundle must do is what separates native Shopify Bundles from a paid bundle app. Nesting, mix-and-match, or bundles that are also subscriptions all fall outside the native app and become a licence line and a build task.
teach.limits: Shopify Bundles: up to 30 components per bundle, no nested bundles, and not compatible with subscriptions or pre-orders. Bundle behaviour in the cart is extended through the Cart Transform Function.

questions.text: Which subscription features are needed?

teach.why: Feature by feature is how you test whether Shopify Subscriptions is enough. Anything it does not cover raises the subscriptions_app signal and adds an app licence, a data migration of existing subscribers and integration work to the backlog.

questions.text: For pre-orders, when is the customer charged?
questions.help: Pre-orders need a pre-order app; express checkouts (Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay) are not available for pre-orders.

native.plan_note: Shopify Payments or PayPal Express only

teach.why: Pre-orders run on selling plans and always need an app, and the charge timing decides the payment set-up: deferred payment is restricted to Shopify Payments or PayPal Express, and express checkout buttons do not appear on pre-orders.

options.pros: Cash up front and no deferred-payment gateway restriction.
options.cons: Higher refund exposure if the release date slips.

options.pros: Customer only pays when the product ships, which lifts conversion on long lead times.
options.cons: Tied to Shopify Payments or PayPal Express, and failed charges at fulfilment have to be handled.

teach.limits: Pre-orders need an app. Shopify Payments or PayPal Express only, and Shop Pay, Apple Pay and Google Pay are not available for pre-orders.

questions.text: Do customers personalise products with choices that are not stock variants (engraving, file upload, paid add-ons, configurators)?

teach.why: Engraving, uploads, paid add-ons and configurators are not stock variants, so they do not consume the three-option or variant limits. They need a product options app and usually theme work, which is a licence and a build item, not a configuration task.
teach.limits: Shopify has no native product personalisation; this is app territory (Custom products category).

questions.text: Roughly how many collections?

teach.why: Collection count sizes the merchandising set-up and the navigation build, and tells you how much of the catalogue structure has to be recreated or migrated rather than generated by rules.

questions.text: Are collections manual, rule-based (automated), or mixed?

teach.why: Automated collections are built from conditions on product data, so they only work if the product data carries the fields the rules need. The answer tells you how much merchandising is ongoing manual work and how much is a one-off data model job.

options.pros: Products join and leave collections automatically as product data changes; little day-to-day upkeep.
options.cons: Depends on clean, consistent product data, so it pushes work into attributes and tagging.

options.pros: Full merchandising control and exact ordering, with no dependency on data quality.
options.cons: Every new product has to be placed by hand, which does not scale with a large catalogue.

questions.text: Which product attributes go beyond Shopify's standard fields (technical specs, certifications, fit guides, ingredients)?
questions.help: Shopify stores extra attributes as metafields and metaobjects and uses the Standard Product Taxonomy for category attributes (filters, Google and Meta feeds). With a PIM, attributes come from the PIM.

native.plan_note: Metaobject definitions: 128 below Plus, 256 on Plus

teach.why: Anything beyond Shopify's standard product fields becomes metafields and metaobjects, and category attributes come from the Standard Product Taxonomy. This list drives the data model, the storefront filters, the Google and Meta feeds, and the SKU complexity gate.
teach.limits: Metaobject definitions are capped at 128 below Plus and 256 on Plus. Category metafields come from the Standard Product Taxonomy.

questions.text: Where is catalogue data maintained today?
questions.help: Typical: products and content from the PIM; prices and inventory from the ERP.

teach.why: Where product data is mastered decides the integration work: a PIM or ERP as the source means Shopify is a target system and needs a sync for products, prices and stock, rather than merchants editing in the admin.

questions.text: Which attributes should shoppers filter by on collection and search pages?
questions.help: Shopify Search & Discovery: up to 25 filters; no filters on collections over 5,000 products.

native.feature: Search & Discovery: storefront filters, up to 25 per store
Predictive search, product boosts and synonyms

teach.why: Filters are built from product data — options, metafields and taxonomy attributes — so the filter list is really a data requirement. It also decides whether native Search & Discovery is enough or a search app enters the cost model.

options.pros: First-party, no licence fee, configured in the admin.
options.cons: Capped at 25 filters and unavailable on collections over 5,000 products.

options.pros: Handles large collections, more filters and merchandising rules on search results.
options.cons: Monthly licence, a catalogue index to keep in sync, and theme integration work.

teach.limits: Search & Discovery shows at most 25 filters per store and 100 values per filter, and each source can be used once. Two ceilings decide whether it is enough at all: a collection over 5,000 products shows no filters, and search results over 100,000 show none either. Filters come from product options, metafields and the standard attributes taxonomy, so the filter set is a product-data decision before it is a storefront one.

questions.text: Are there special prices for consumer groups (VIP or member prices)?
questions.help: Prices for business customers are covered in § 6.2. Consumer group prices use discounts for customer segments or an app.

native.plan_note: Up to 3 active catalogs below Plus

teach.why: Member and VIP prices for consumers are not a native price list: they are delivered as discounts on customer segments or with an app. Confirm whether they mean consumer groups or business customers, because business pricing runs on B2B catalogs instead (section 6.2).
teach.limits: B2B catalogs are capped at 3 active catalogs below Plus; catalogs assigned directly to a company or location are Plus only.

questions.text: Are there volume offers for shoppers (e.g. 3 for 2, tiered discounts)?
questions.help: Automatic discounts and buy X get Y cover most volume offers natively. Business volume pricing is covered in § 6.2.

teach.why: Three for two and tiered offers are usually automatic discounts or buy X get Y, which are native and configured, not built. The answer decides whether promotions are a set-up task or a Shopify Function build in the backlog.
teach.limits: Applying several product discounts to one item is a Plus feature (exit rule 11.1).

questions.text: Do prices differ by market (not just currency conversion)?
questions.help: Shopify Markets supports percentage adjustments, fixed prices per product per country and price rounding.

teach.why: Currency conversion alone is automatic; genuinely different prices per market are a Shopify Markets catalogue job, using percentage adjustments, rounding rules or fixed prices per product per country. That changes how the price feed from the ERP has to be built.
teach.limits: Shopify Markets offers percentage adjustment per market, rounding rules, and fixed prices per product by country or region. A fixed price takes precedence over any other adjustment, and price list currency must match the market's.

questions.text: Where is the inventory source of truth — Shopify, ERP, WMS, other?
questions.help: With the ERP as source of truth, Shopify still needs stock per location.

teach.why: The source of truth decides the direction of the stock integration and who resolves conflicts. Even when the ERP or WMS owns stock, Shopify still needs a quantity per location, so the feed has to be location-aware, not a single total.

options.pros: No inbound stock sync; merchants adjust stock in the admin and the storefront is always accurate.
options.cons: Does not fit if the warehouse or retail systems already move stock outside Shopify.

options.option: ERP or WMS as source of truth
options.pros: One stock figure across all channels, owned by the system that actually holds the goods.
options.cons: Needs a per-location feed into Shopify, and sync latency shows up as overselling.

questions.text: Are low-stock alerts needed?
questions.help: Shopify has no built-in low-stock alert; we set it up with Shopify Flow.

teach.why: Shopify does not send low-stock alerts out of the box. If the client expects them, it is a Shopify Flow workflow to build and maintain, so it belongs in the backlog rather than being assumed as a setting.

questions.text: What should happen when a product is out of stock?
questions.help: Continue selling (backorder) is native; back-in-stock alerts and pre-orders need apps.

native.feature: Continue selling when out of stock

teach.why: Out-of-stock behaviour splits cleanly: continuing to sell (backorder) is a native product setting, while back-in-stock alerts and pre-orders both need apps. The answer raises the back_in_stock_app and pre_order_app signals and their licences.
teach.limits: Continue selling when out of stock is native from Basic. Back-in-stock alerts and pre-orders require apps.

questions.text: Which inventory tasks will your team do in Shopify?
questions.help: Purchase orders, transfers and stock adjustments are native in Shopify admin (Stocky is retired).

teach.why: Purchase orders, transfers and stock adjustments are native in the Shopify admin, so this answer tells you how much of the client's stock operation moves into Shopify, which drives training, roles and permissions rather than build effort.

questions.text: Which countries do you sell to at launch? For each: the country, the currency customers pay in, the languages, the web address customers use there today, how prices are set, which of your companies invoices the customer, whether the range is the same as in your main country, and who runs that country day to day.
questions.help: One row per country. Leave a cell blank if you do not know it — we will come back to it.

native.feature: Shopify Markets (no limit on country markets)

native.plan_note: 20 languages below Plus, 30 on Plus

teach.why: Sets the whole international scope: markets, currencies, languages, domains and price strategy. The entity, range and owner columns are what the engine reads to decide one store with Markets, expansion stores or a hybrid — the client is never asked to choose the topology.
teach.limits: Shopify documents no limit on the number of country or region markets. Published languages are capped at 20 below Plus and 30 on Plus. Charging in a local currency (rather than only displaying one) requires Shopify Payments or Adyen; with any other provider the customer is charged in the store's default currency. Mainland China is excluded from this engagement and routed to a separate China discovery.

questions.why_it_matters: These rows decide how many Shopify stores your business needs. Countries that share one selling company, one range and one team can run on a single store; countries that differ on those points usually need their own store, which multiplies the build, the running cost and the work of every future change.
questions.what_good_looks_like: One row per launch country, with the invoicing company named even when it is the same everywhere, and the range marked same, subset or different. A vague answer sounds like "Europe" or "the usual countries". The follow-up that sharpens it: "which company name appears on the invoice a customer in that country receives?"
questions.who_can_answer: Country manager or commercial lead for the range and the team; the controller for the invoicing company.

unknown_path.fallback: Markets with no selling entity are assumed to sell through the headquarters entity (Q1.1.2); a blank assortment is assumed to be the same range as the primary market; a blank owner is assumed to be the central team.
unknown_path.assumption: One selling entity, one range, one team across all markets — the single-store case.
unknown_path.resolve_by: Name the invoicing company per country with the controller, and the range owner per country with the commercial lead.

questions.text: Which are the primary markets (one or more country or market codes)?
questions.help: The markets that lead revenue and launch priority, e.g. US and EU for a global brand.

teach.why: Primary markets decide which currency, domain, payment methods and tax set-up get the design effort and get tested first. Every other market is sequenced behind them, and the roll-out waves are built from this answer.

questions.text: Which countries are planned in the next 12 months?

teach.why: A market added later is cheap if the domain, catalogue and pricing structure anticipated it, and expensive if it forces a re-cut. It also shows whether the plan you choose today survives the next twelve months.
teach.limits: Domain strategy is the hardest thing to change later: subfolders inherit the main domain's search ranking, while a ccTLD builds its own authority from scratch. Deleting a market later needs redirects or customers hit 404s.

questions.text: Stated preference only — does the client already have a view on running all countries from one store or giving some countries their own store? Record it as their view, not as the answer.
questions.help: Recorded as a stated preference. It never decides the recommendation; where it differs, the closing document argues the gap.

native.plan_note: Up to 9 expansion stores

teach.why: This is the one question in the bank that asks for an opinion rather than a fact, and it is kept only so the closing document can address the client's own view. The topology itself is derived from the business facts in Q3.1.1, Q1.1.6, Q3.4.2, Q3.4.13, Q5.1.3 and Q6.2.14.

options.pros: One admin, one catalogue, one theme; per-market currency, domain, language, catalogue and tax overrides; available from Basic; no duplicated app bills
options.cons: Shared catalogue structure and app stack; per-market theme content needs Advanced or higher; one legal entity unless the client is on Plus

options.pros: Each region runs its own catalogue, apps, team and settings — suits separately run regional businesses or different legal entities
options.cons: Plus only; products, collections, inventory and settings are not synced; apps billed per store, theme licences not shared; every change is done more than once

teach.limits: Never let this answer stand in for the analysis. Expansion stores need Shopify Plus and duplicate every catalogue, theme and app change; one store with Markets keeps them together but shares one theme, one app estate and one admin.

questions.why_it_matters: If you already have a view, we will say where the evidence agrees with it and where it does not, rather than quietly designing around it.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A view the client actually holds, with the reason they hold it. Leave it blank when they have none — a blank is better than a guess.
questions.who_can_answer: Ecommerce director or CTO, where one has already formed a view.

unknown_path.fallback: No stated preference is recorded and the computed recommendation stands alone.
unknown_path.assumption: None — absence of a preference costs nothing.
unknown_path.resolve_by: Nothing to resolve; this is an opinion, not a fact.

questions.text: How should visitors reach their local market?
questions.help: Automatic redirection is native; EU visitors on EU country domains are not redirected automatically.

native.plan_note: The Geolocation app is retired

teach.why: Clients assume visitors always land in the right market. Automatic redirection is native and free, but it has documented gaps that show up as the wrong currency on a live site, so agree the behaviour now.

options.pros: Right currency, language and prices on first view; native, no app, no build
options.cons: Does not apply to EU visitors already on an EU ccTLD; annoys customers who deliberately want another market unless a selector is also offered

options.option: Show a country and language selector only
options.pros: The customer chooses and keeps their choice; a selector is needed anyway when selling in local currencies
options.cons: Some customers never use it and shop in the wrong currency; higher bounce on paid traffic landing from another country

teach.limits: Customers from the EU arriving on an EU country-code domain (ccTLD) are not redirected automatically. Language redirection only works where the language is added, assigned, translated and published. Content on markets using shared domains is not indexed by search engines. The old Geolocation app is retired; it only ever recommended a market rather than switching it.

questions.text: Should any market have its own theme content, section order, checkout or customer-account settings?

teach.why: Per-market theme content requires the Advanced plan or higher. On Basic or Grow every market shares one theme customisation, so a yes here can move the plan — and the client's monthly cost — before any design work starts.
teach.limits: Adaptation fields may appear in Translate & Adapt on lower plans but will not display. Changing the information, shipping or payment steps of checkout, or restyling checkout through the Checkout Branding API, is Plus only; extensions on the thank-you and order-status pages work from Basic. A separate legal entity per market is Plus only.

questions.text: Are some products not allowed to be sold in certain markets (regulation, registration, licensing or distribution agreements)?
questions.help: List them in a note. In Shopify, products are excluded from the catalog of that market.

native.feature: Market catalogs: include or exclude products per market

teach.why: Market catalogs include or exclude products per market, so a licensing, registration or distribution restriction is configuration rather than custom code. But it has to be known before the catalogue structure and price lists are designed.
teach.limits: Shopify does not police this — the exclusion is a catalogue setting the client maintains as the range changes. Where a parent market and a submarket both price a product, the more specific price is used. Catalogue customisation for retail markets needs Shopify POS Pro or Plus.

questions.text: How will translation be handled?
questions.help: Translate & Adapt (Shopify's free app) auto-translates up to 2 languages; more languages need manual work or a translation app. Checkout is pre-translated.

native.plan_note: Auto-translates at most 2 languages; not policies

teach.why: Translate & Adapt is free but auto-translates at most two languages, and once a language is used that choice cannot be switched. Beyond two, translation becomes a recurring human or app cost, not a one-off build task.

options.pros: Free, native, no extra app in the stack; machine translation for up to two languages; per-market adaptation of the same content
options.cons: Two auto-translated languages maximum and the choice is locked; policies and URL handles stay manual; no translator workflow, review or memory

options.option: A translation app (for example Weglot, Langify, Transcy)
options.pros: More languages, translation memory, glossaries and review workflows; usually covers app and theme strings Translate & Adapt misses
options.cons: A monthly cost that scales with words and languages; another dependency in the theme and in checkout-adjacent content; quality still needs review

options.option: Human or agency translation loaded into Shopify
options.pros: Brand-quality copy, transcreation for each market, full control of tone and legal wording
options.cons: Slowest and most expensive; needs an owner for every content change; without an app the loading and re-loading is manual work forever

teach.limits: Translate & Adapt covers products, collections, blog posts, policies and pages, but does not auto-translate policies or URL handles. Checkout is pre-translated by Shopify. Published languages are capped at 20 below Plus and 30 on Plus. The fourth language and beyond is priced as scope — the first three are in every offer, because a Swiss engagement is DE/FR/IT. More than six is a stop rule: translation and content operations move to a Discovery Phase.

questions.text: Does any language need right-to-left layout?

teach.why: Right-to-left is a theme engineering question, not a translation one — layout, navigation, icons, forms and email templates all mirror. It changes theme effort and the test matrix, so it cannot surface after the design is signed off.

questions.text: Is SEO per language a priority?

teach.why: Each published language gets its own URL and hreflang tags are added automatically, so the native baseline is decent. The real work is translated metadata, handles and content, which decides whether an app or a human translator is needed.
teach.limits: Published languages appear in sitemaps and hreflang is automatic for language-specific URLs. Translate & Adapt does not auto-translate URL handles. Markets that use shared domains are not indexed by search engines, so check the domain strategy before promising local SEO.

questions.text: What must be translated?
questions.help: Translate & Adapt does not auto-translate policies or URL handles.

teach.why: Scope decides cost. Product and collection text is one job; policies, URL handles, metafields, emails, theme strings and app content are another. Translate & Adapt does not auto-translate policies or URL handles, so those stay manual or app work.
teach.limits: Translate & Adapt covers products, collections, blog posts, policies and pages — but its machine translation is limited to two languages and excludes policies and URL handles. Checkout itself is already translated by Shopify.

questions.text: Should duties and import taxes be collected at checkout (DDP)?
questions.help: Duties and import taxes can be charged at checkout (DDP) or paid by the customer on delivery (DAP), chosen per country. Needs HS codes (and country of origin) on products; not combinable with tax overrides, manual tax rates or customer tax exemptions; DDP labels only with some carriers.

native.feature: Duties and import taxes at checkout (DDP or DAP per country)
native.plan_note: Plan not stated by Shopify; fee per order; not with tax overrides, manual rates or exemptions

teach.why: DDP means the customer pays import costs at checkout and nothing on delivery; DAP means a courier bill at the door and refused parcels. It is a commercial and service decision with hard technical prerequisites behind it.

options.option: Collect duties and import taxes at checkout (DDP)
options.pros: No surprise bill on delivery, so fewer refused parcels and support tickets; total price is honest at checkout; a better cross-border experience
options.cons: Needs HS codes and country of origin on every product and a carrier supporting DDP labels; a per-order fee; rules out tax overrides, manual rates and exemptions; higher price shown at checkout hurts conversion

options.option: Leave duties to the customer on delivery (DAP)
options.pros: Nothing to configure, no product customs data needed, no per-order duty fee, lowest price shown at checkout
options.cons: Customers get an unexpected courier invoice; refused deliveries, returns and chargebacks; the brand takes the blame for a cost it never disclosed

teach.limits: DDP needs HS codes (and country of origin) on products and a carrier that supports DDP labels. It is not compatible with tax overrides, manual tax rates or customer tax exemptions. You cannot offer both DDP and DAP in the same country. No duties in the Rest of world shipping zone, and twelve countries and regions are unsupported, including Northern Ireland. Charges are estimates at the time of order. Duties and taxes are collected together — taxes cannot be collected alone. Fee: 0.85% with Shopify Payments, 1.5% with other providers, on orders with duties calculated. Without a DDP label, the customer is still charged on delivery.

questions.text: In which countries are you VAT-registered?

teach.why: Registrations are entered per region in Shopify and decide which VAT is charged where. Without the registration Shopify cannot collect that country's VAT at checkout — no configuration works around a registration the client does not hold.
teach.limits: Shopify Tax covers the United States, European Union, United Kingdom and Canada. Outside those, Basic Tax covers Norway, Switzerland, Australia, New Zealand and Singapore, and requires a tax registration number. Shopify calculates but never files or remits — that stays with the client and their tax adviser.

questions.text: Do you sell into the US with state sales tax obligations?

teach.why: US sales tax obligations are decided state by state by the client's own sales, not by Shopify. The answer tells you whether US registrations and rates are in scope and whether a tax adviser is needed before launch.
teach.limits: Shopify Tax covers the United States, and calculates rates, but the client is responsible for registering, filing and remitting. Shopify does not file or remit anywhere.

questions.text: Do products have HS codes and country of origin, and where do they come from?

teach.why: No HS codes, no duties at checkout. This tells you whether the data exists at all, where it is mastered — ERP, PIM or supplier — and whether a data workstream sits on the critical path to a DDP launch.
teach.limits: Shopify requires HS codes applied to products (with country of origin) before duties and import taxes can be calculated at checkout. Under Managed Markets, Global-e assigns HS codes automatically instead.

questions.text: Should prices include tax (VAT) in some markets and exclude it in others?
questions.help: Shopify can show tax-inclusive prices per market (dynamic tax display).

teach.why: European shoppers expect a VAT-inclusive price; US shoppers expect tax added at checkout. Shopify handles both from one price with dynamic tax-inclusive pricing, so this is a configuration answer, not a second set of price lists.
teach.limits: Dynamic tax-inclusive pricing is set per market and is documented from the Basic plan. It changes the displayed price, so confirm the resulting round numbers in each market with the client — rounding rules are Shopify's defaults and cannot be customised.

questions.text: Which tax service?
questions.help: Shopify Tax covers the US, EU, UK and Canada; since 2026-05-13 new stores selling in the EU, UK or Canada cannot use Basic Tax.

native.plan_note: Basic Tax closed to new EU, UK and Canada stores since 2026-05-13

teach.why: For most European clients this is not really a choice: since 13 May 2026 new stores selling in the EU, UK or Canada cannot use Basic Tax. Shopify Tax calculates, but it never files or remits.

options.pros: Native, no integration to build or maintain; rates for the US, EU, UK and Canada; product categories give reduced rates and exemptions; free up to a sales threshold
options.cons: Per-order fee above the threshold; only four regions covered; no filing or remittance; nothing outside those regions unless Basic Tax applies

options.option: A third-party tax service (for example TaxJar)
options.pros: Covers regions and edge cases Shopify Tax does not; usually adds filing and remittance workflows the client may already use with their accountant
options.cons: Another subscription and another integration to test and maintain; duplicates work Shopify Tax already does in its four regions; the tax logic now lives in two places

teach.limits: Shopify Tax covers the United States, European Union, United Kingdom and Canada. Outside those, Basic Tax covers Norway, Switzerland, Australia, New Zealand and Singapore and requires a tax registration number. Shopify Tax is free up to a sales threshold, then charged per order with a cap. Filing and remittance always stay with the client.

questions.text: Do business customers buy tax-exempt (VAT number validation, reverse charge)?
questions.help: VAT ID validation at checkout is native.

teach.why: VAT ID validation at checkout is native, so reverse charge is configuration rather than a build. But the answer decides whether B2B buyers need their own market, customer group and catalogue — which reshapes pricing and the tax set-up.
teach.limits: Managed Markets does not support B2B orders, so a client needing both tax-exempt B2B trade and an outsourced merchant of record cannot have both. Selling B2B in more than one currency requires Shopify Payments.

questions.text: In which countries should duties and import taxes be collected at checkout (DDP)? In the others the customer pays on delivery (DAP).
questions.help: Countries, e.g. United States, United Kingdom, Switzerland. One choice per country: DDP and DAP can't both be offered in the same country. If you don't ship across borders, say so in a comment.

native.feature: DDP or DAP per country or region
native.plan_note: Not available for some destinations (e.g. Northern Ireland) or the Rest of world zone

teach.why: DDP is chosen per country and you cannot offer both DDP and DAP in the same country. The list drives shipping profiles, carrier choice and the per-order duty fee, so it belongs in scope rather than in go-live week.
teach.limits: Twelve countries and regions are unsupported, including Northern Ireland, Russia and Puerto Rico, and duties cannot be charged in the Rest of world shipping zone. Duties and taxes are collected together — taxes alone is not an option. DDP labels bought through Shopify's own carrier accounts are limited to Canada Post (US destinations only) and DHL Express (US and Canada); DHL eCommerce is DAP only. Other carriers must be confirmed directly.

questions.text: When you ship low-value parcels into these territories from outside them, are you registered to collect the import VAT or GST at checkout?
questions.help: Low-value parcels into the EU (IOSS), the UK, Switzerland, Norway (VOEC), Australia and New Zealand. Tick the schemes you are registered for.

native.feature: Low-value goods taxes (EU, UK, Switzerland, Norway, Australia, New Zealand)
native.plan_note: Registration needed; Shopify recommends DDP so orders above the threshold get duties calculated

native.feature: EU IOSS: collect VAT at checkout on low-value orders

teach.why: This is the classic over-promise. Shopify can only collect EU import VAT at checkout on low-value orders if the client holds an IOSS registration. The same applies to the UK, Swiss, Norwegian VOEC, Australian and New Zealand schemes.
teach.limits: IOSS is for merchants outside the EU selling to EU customers, and lets them collect VAT at checkout on orders of €150 or less. Registration is optional in principle but required if VAT is to be charged during checkout. OSS registrations do not apply when the fulfilment location is outside the EU. Shopify recommends DDP alongside these schemes so orders above the threshold still get duties calculated. Shopify also documents that from 1 July 2026 the EU begins removing the €150 customs duty exemption — confirm the current position for the client's goods.

questions.text: Do some products have reduced or zero tax rates, or tax exemptions, in any market (e.g. medicines, books, food, children's clothing)?
questions.help: Finance confirms the rates; Merkle does not give tax advice.

native.feature: Product categories for reduced rates and exemptions (Shopify Tax: US, EU, UK)
Product tax overrides per country or state (manual collections)
native.plan_note: Ignored where duties are collected at checkout

teach.why: Reduced and zero rates are driven by product category in Shopify Tax, or by manual tax overrides. The answer decides whether the product data needs a tax category field — and it is Finance's call, never ours.
teach.limits: Product categories for reduced rates and exemptions apply to Shopify Tax in the US, EU and UK. Manual product tax overrides are set per country or state, but are ignored where duties are collected at checkout and are not compatible with DDP at all. Merkle does not give tax advice: the client's finance team or adviser confirms every rate.

questions.text: Who issues invoices to customers?
questions.help: Shopify can generate VAT invoices for EU and UK orders (shown on the order status page, not emailed, not for orders with duties). The free Order Printer app prints invoices from templates. Invoices can also come from the ERP or an invoicing app.

native.feature: VAT invoices for EU and UK orders
native.plan_note: Shopify Tax; not emailed; not for orders with duties; Portugal not supported

teach.why: Shopify's VAT invoices cover EU and UK orders only, appear on the order status page rather than by email, and are not produced for orders with duties. Most cross-border clients therefore need an app or their ERP.

options.option: Shopify native VAT invoices plus Order Printer
options.pros: Free and native; no extra app cost; enough for a simple EU or UK business with no duties at checkout
options.cons: EU and UK orders only; not emailed to the customer; nothing for orders with duties; Portugal unsupported; no e-invoicing formats

options.option: An invoicing app (for example Sufio, Order Printer Pro)
options.pros: Automatic emailed invoices, credit notes, branding, per-country numbering, and in some apps the EU e-invoicing formats
options.cons: A monthly cost and another app holding order and customer data; invoice numbering rules must still be agreed with the client's finance team

options.option: The client's ERP or finance system issues invoices
options.pros: One source of truth for accounting, numbering and credit notes; already audited; handles e-invoicing mandates the client faces elsewhere
options.cons: Needs an order integration and a defined timing rule; invoices are late if the integration lags; customer service must know where to find them

teach.limits: Native VAT invoices require Shopify Tax, are not emailed, are not generated for orders that include duties, and Portugal is not supported. The free Shopify Order Printer app prints invoices and packing slips from templates but is a document tool, not a compliance one.

questions.text: Which electronic invoicing (e-invoicing) obligations apply to your sales?
questions.help: For example Peppol, XRechnung or ZUGFeRD (Germany), Factur-X (France), SdI (Italy), KSeF (Poland) or VeriFactu (Spain). Shopify has no built-in e-invoicing: it comes from the ERP or an invoicing app.

native.feature: VAT invoices for EU and UK orders (not e-invoicing)

teach.why: Shopify has no built-in e-invoicing. Peppol, XRechnung, ZUGFeRD, Factur-X, SdI, KSeF and VeriFactu are all ERP or app work, so a mandate in any market becomes a named integration with a legal deadline attached.
teach.limits: Shopify's native VAT invoices for EU and UK orders are documents, not e-invoices, and do not satisfy any of these schemes. Confirm each obligation with the client's finance team or tax adviser — Merkle does not give tax advice.

questions.text: If selling in a country meant registering for tax there and filing returns, would you take that on yourself, or would you rather a partner were the legal seller for those orders?
questions.help: Answer for the countries you sell to but are not registered in today.
questions.why_it_matters: This decides who carries the tax and customs liability on cross-border orders. Keeping it yourself means registering, filing and remitting in each country; handing it to a partner removes that work and that risk, and costs a percentage of every international order.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A position the finance function actually holds, ideally with the countries they will and will not register in. A vague answer sounds like "whatever is easiest". The follow-up that sharpens it: "who files your VAT returns today, and how many countries is that?"
questions.who_can_answer: Controller, head of finance or the external tax adviser.

unknown_path.fallback: Assumed own_registrations: the business keeps its registrations and Shopify Markets handles duties and taxes itself.
unknown_path.assumption: The client is willing to register where it sells.
unknown_path.resolve_by: One conversation with the controller about where they file today and where they refuse to.

native.feature: Shopify Tax and Basic Tax registrations per region

teach.why: Together with the market list and the current registrations (Q3.4.2), this decides the cross-border model: self-managed duties on Shopify Markets, or a merchant of record. It replaces the retired Q3.1.6, which asked the client to name a model they had never heard of.
teach.limits: Managed Markets is the only merchant-of-record route inside Shopify, and it is open only to businesses in the continental United States and certain stores in Canada and the United Kingdom, on Shopify Payments, and it does not support B2B. For everyone else the honest options are self-managed registrations or a third-party merchant-of-record app.

questions.text: Do you want to sell to mainland China cross-border (from outside China) or onshore, behind the Great Firewall?
questions.help: Onshore selling needs a PRC entity, an ICP filing or licence and hosting in China.

native.feature: Shopify in China: Shopify's servers are not located in mainland China

teach.why: Shopify's servers are not located in mainland China, and selling onshore needs a PRC entity, an ICP filing or licence and local hosting. This answer routes China to a separate discovery — it is outside this engagement's scope.

options.option: Cross-border into China (from outside the mainland)
options.pros: No PRC entity, ICP filing or onshore hosting needed; can start through marketplaces or a Hong Kong store; customs channels are designed for it
options.cons: Per-order and yearly limits per consumer; goods must be on the cross-border positive list; marketplace fees and a local partner; Shopify is rarely the storefront the customer sees

options.pros: A normal Chinese shopping experience, domestic payment and logistics, no customs limits per shopper, full local marketing integration
options.cons: Needs a PRC legal entity, an ICP filing or commercial licence and hosting inside China — Shopify has no infrastructure in mainland China, so it cannot be the platform; months of lead time and PRC counsel

teach.limits: Mainland China is not part of the Merkle offering. Naming China as a launch market flags the engagement for a separate China discovery and removes China from this engagement's markets, languages, offer, plan and build scope. If mainland China is the only launch market, this engagement stops and becomes a China discovery.

questions.text: Which channels for mainland China?
questions.help: Cross-border marketplaces (Tmall Global, JD Worldwide, Douyin Global, RED), a WeChat mini-program, your own site, or a Hong Kong store shipping to the mainland.

teach.why: Each China channel is a different build: a cross-border marketplace, a WeChat mini-program, a Hong Kong store. Shopify is not the storefront in most of them, so this answer sizes the separate China discovery, not this engagement.
teach.limits: Shopify has no native China marketplace or WeChat channel; connectors such as the WalkTheChat apps sit between Shopify and those channels. Mainland China is excluded from this engagement's scope regardless of the channel chosen.

questions.text: Do you have a legal entity in mainland China?
questions.help: Needed for an ICP filing or licence and for onshore hosting.

teach.why: No PRC entity means no ICP filing and no onshore hosting, so selling onshore is off the table before any technical discussion starts. It is the first fact the separate China discovery needs from the client.
teach.limits: Shopify cannot host a site inside mainland China in any case — its servers are not located there — so an entity alone does not make Shopify the onshore platform.

questions.text: Do you have a Hong Kong or other overseas entity that can sell cross-border, and are your trademarks registered in China?
questions.help: Cross-border marketplaces require both.

teach.why: Cross-border marketplaces require both an overseas selling entity and trademarks registered in China. Without them the cross-border route is blocked on paperwork with long lead times, which the separate China discovery has to plan around.
teach.limits: This is a legal and brand-protection question, not a Shopify one. Merkle does not give PRC legal advice; the client's counsel confirms entity and trademark status.

questions.text: ICP status for a China website?
questions.help: Your PRC counsel confirms whether a filing is enough or a commercial ICP licence is needed.

teach.why: An ICP filing or a commercial ICP licence decides whether a China-hosted website is legally possible and how long it takes. Shopify cannot host it, so the answer belongs to the separate China discovery.
teach.limits: Shopify's servers are not located in mainland China, so an ICP filing does not turn a Shopify store into an onshore China site. The client's PRC counsel confirms whether a filing is enough or a commercial licence is needed.

questions.text: What is Shopify's role for mainland China?
questions.help: Shopify can stay the global master for products, inventory and orders while China sells through local channels.

native.feature: Shopify in China: Shopify's servers are not located in mainland China

teach.why: Even where China sells through local channels, Shopify can stay the global master for products, inventory and orders. This answer defines the integration surface between this engagement and the separate China workstream.

options.option: Shopify stays the global master for products, inventory and orders
options.pros: One catalogue and one stock picture; China channels are fed from the same data; reporting stays consolidated
options.cons: Needs connectors and a China-specific data mapping; China channels impose their own attributes, claims rules and image requirements

options.option: China runs entirely separately from Shopify
options.pros: No integration work in this engagement; the local partner owns the stack the local market expects
options.cons: Two catalogues, two stock pictures and no consolidated reporting; the brand loses direct sight of Chinese customers and demand

teach.limits: Shopify has no infrastructure in mainland China, so it cannot be the onshore storefront. Keeping it as the master system is a data and integration decision, not a selling one.

questions.text: How will goods enter China: bonded warehouse (1210), direct mail (9610), general trade, or personal parcels?
questions.help: Cross-border channels have per-order and yearly limits per consumer.

teach.why: Bonded warehouse, direct mail, general trade and personal parcels carry different duties, paperwork and per-order and yearly limits per consumer. None of it is Shopify configuration; it sizes the separate China discovery.
teach.limits: Cross-border channels have per-order and yearly limits per consumer. This is customs and logistics work owned by the client's trade partner and PRC advisers, not by the Shopify build.

questions.text: Are your products on China's cross-border e-commerce positive list?

teach.why: Goods off China's cross-border e-commerce positive list cannot move through the bonded or direct-mail channels, which can remove the whole cross-border route for a catalogue. It is a product fact, not a platform one.
teach.limits: The positive list is set by Chinese authorities and changes. The client's trade partner or PRC counsel confirms it — Merkle does not.

questions.text: How are your products classified in China?
questions.help: Whitening, sunscreen and anti-hair-loss products are special cosmetics; medicines are not cross-border goods.

teach.why: China treats whitening, sunscreen and anti-hair-loss products as special cosmetics, and medicines are not cross-border goods at all. Classification decides which channel is even legal, so it comes before any China technical planning.
teach.limits: Classification is a Chinese regulatory judgement confirmed by the client's PRC counsel or trade partner, and it can differ from how the same product is classified in the EU or US.

questions.text: Registration or filing status with China's medical products administration (NMPA)?
questions.help: General trade needs registration or filing; cross-border channels are exempt for goods on the positive list.

teach.why: General trade needs NMPA registration or filing; cross-border channels are exempt for goods on the positive list. The answer sets the lead time to a China launch and belongs in the separate China discovery.
teach.limits: Registration and filing timelines are set by the Chinese authorities and can run to months. Merkle does not provide PRC regulatory advice.

questions.text: Do product claims need a review for China (medical, cosmeceutical or treatment claims)?
questions.help: China does not allow cosmeceutical or medical claims for cosmetics.

teach.why: China does not allow cosmeceutical or medical claims for cosmetics, so copy translated straight from the global site can be non-compliant. It is a content workstream the separate China discovery has to own and resource.
teach.limits: This is a legal review of product claims, not a translation task. Approval sits with the client's PRC counsel or trade partner.

questions.text: How will mainland customers pay?
questions.help: Inside the marketplace, Alipay and WeChat Pay through a Hong Kong Shopify Payments account (early access), a cross-border wallet provider, or domestic merchant accounts (PRC entity).

native.plan_note: Hong Kong SAR Shopify Payments account; early access; customers pay in CNY; no chargebacks
Hong Kong SAR Shopify Payments account; early access

teach.why: Alipay and WeChat Pay are available through a Hong Kong Shopify Payments account in early access; domestic merchant accounts need a PRC entity. This answer decides whether a Shopify-hosted China checkout is possible at all.
teach.limits: Both methods require a Hong Kong SAR Shopify Payments account and are in early access. Customers pay in CNY. WeChat Pay has no chargebacks. Inside a marketplace, payment is the marketplace's, not Shopify's.

questions.text: How many mainland China customers do you expect per year?
questions.help: China's personal information law sets different data-export obligations by volume.

teach.why: China's personal information law sets different data-export obligations by volume, so the expected customer count decides which compliance regime applies. Nothing about it is a Shopify setting; it feeds the separate China discovery.
teach.limits: Shopify's servers are not located in mainland China, so every China customer record is a cross-border transfer by default. The client's PRC counsel confirms the obligations.

questions.text: Do you have a representative in China for personal information protection (PIPL)?
questions.help: Required when an offshore business targets consumers in China.

teach.why: PIPL requires a representative in China when an offshore business targets Chinese consumers. It is a named legal appointment the client must make, not a platform setting, and it gates a compliant China launch.
teach.limits: Merkle does not provide PRC legal advice; the appointment and its terms come from the client's counsel.

questions.text: Where will China customer data (CRM, email, analytics) be stored?

teach.why: Where China customer data sits decides whether a cross-border transfer mechanism is needed and which CRM, email and analytics tools may be used at all. Shopify's servers are not in mainland China.
teach.limits: Several common martech tools are unreachable or unlawful for China data, so the answer can change the whole stack for that market. The client's PRC counsel confirms the transfer mechanism.

questions.text: Must scripts blocked in China (Google Fonts, Google Analytics, reCAPTCHA, Meta pixels, YouTube) be replaced?

native.feature: Shopify notes that firewalls in China frequently block Google Fonts

teach.why: Google Fonts, Google Analytics, reCAPTCHA, Meta pixels and YouTube are commonly blocked in China — Shopify itself notes that firewalls there frequently block Google Fonts. Every replacement is real theme and tracking build work.
teach.limits: Blocked scripts do not fail quietly: they can stall page rendering for Chinese visitors even on a site that works everywhere else. Shopify documents the Google Fonts case; the rest must be tested from inside China.

questions.text: Which marketing channels for China?

teach.why: China's marketing stack is entirely local — different platforms, different tracking, different content formats. The answer sizes the separate China discovery and shows how much of the global martech investment carries over. Usually very little.
teach.limits: Shopify's marketing integrations are built for Western channels; Chinese channels are reached through connectors or the local partner's own tooling.

questions.text: Who provides Chinese-language customer service?

teach.why: Chinese-language service, in China hours, on the channels Chinese customers actually use, is an operating commitment the client must staff. It is a readiness check for the China route, not a Shopify configuration.

questions.text: Do you work with a local partner or trade partner for China? Name it.

teach.why: Most successful China entries run through a trade partner or a local agency. Knowing who they are tells you who owns the storefront, the data and the customer — and what Merkle is actually being asked to deliver.

questions.text: Target launch date for mainland China.

teach.why: ICP filings, trademark registrations and NMPA filings take months. A target date shows whether China is a funded plan or an aspiration, and whether it can be sequenced safely after this engagement's launch.
teach.limits: Mainland China is excluded from this engagement's scope and offer, so this date belongs to the separate China discovery's plan, not to this delivery timeline.

questions.text: Who provides PRC legal, tax and customs advice?
questions.help: Merkle does not provide PRC legal advice.

teach.why: Merkle does not provide PRC legal, tax or customs advice. If nobody is named here, the China route has no owner for its highest-risk decisions and the separate China discovery cannot responsibly start.
teach.limits: Entity set-up, ICP status, customs mode, product classification, claims review and PIPL obligations all need a named PRC adviser. Shopify's documentation covers none of them.

questions.text: Which payment providers will you use (Shopify Payments, Adyen, Stripe, PayPal…)?
questions.help: Shopify Payments is required for some features (Shop Pay Installments, Managed Markets, some Markets pricing); third-party gateways are supported.

native.plan_note: Available in 40 countries

teach.why: The provider decides more than fees. Charging buyers in their own currency requires Shopify Payments or Adyen; with any other provider local prices are display only and the buyer is charged in your store's default currency.

options.pros: Charges buyers in local currency; local payment methods, Shop Pay and fraud analysis come with it; no third-party transaction fee
options.cons: Only in supported countries; the client must hold an eligible entity and bank account there

options.pros: Keeps an existing acquirer relationship and its negotiated rates
options.cons: Local currency becomes display only - the buyer is charged in the store currency; third-party transaction fees apply; fraud analysis needs Grow or above

teach.limits: Shopify Payments is available only in supported countries, each with its own bank account and verification requirements - check the client's entity country before assuming it is an option. Third-party transaction fees apply on all third-party gateways; PayPal and manual payments are excluded when Shopify Payments is active.

questions.text: Which local payment methods are required?

native.feature: Local payment methods via Shopify Payments
