teach.why: Local methods decide conversion market by market. Shopify Payments offers them per country and shows them based on the buyer's location, so what is available is set by Shopify's country page rather than by the build.
teach.limits: The store country's payment-methods page is the source of truth, and the sets differ: Switzerland documents TWINT, Germany documents EPS and BLIK, Austria documents EPS. A method that is not listed needs a third-party gateway, with its own transaction fee.

questions.text: Which buy-now-pay-later options, if any?
questions.help: Shop Pay Installments is available to stores in the US, Canada and the UK.

native.plan_note: US, Canada and UK stores

teach.why: Buy now, pay later moves average order value, and the native option is geographically fixed. Shop Pay Installments covers stores in the US, Canada and the UK only; anywhere else the client needs a third-party provider or app.
teach.limits: Shop Pay Installments: US, Canada and UK stores.

questions.text: Do you need payouts in more than one currency?

teach.why: Being paid in a currency is a separate feature from charging in it, and it is the one that costs a plan. Multi-currency payouts need Advanced or Plus; below that the client still sells internationally but is settled in their domestic currency.

options.option: Payouts in each selling currency (Advanced or Plus)
options.pros: A bank account matching the order currency removes the conversion and its fee; cleaner reconciliation per market
options.cons: Forces Advanced or Plus; a Multi-Currency Payout fee applies to every non-domestic payout; one bank account per currency to open and maintain

options.option: Settle everything in the domestic currency
options.pros: Works on any plan; one bank account; no Multi-Currency Payout fee
options.cons: A currency conversion fee applies to non-domestic transactions; the client carries the FX exposure

teach.limits: Advanced or Plus only. The client needs a business entity and bank account in an eligible region, only the store owner can activate it, and there is one bank account per supported payout currency. A Multi-Currency Payout fee applies to any payout in a non-domestic currency; domestic payouts carry none.

questions.text: Will card data be handled only by Shopify-hosted checkout, by a third-party hosted payment page, or by custom card UI / tokenisation?
questions.help: Card data handled outside Shopify-hosted checkout needs a separate security review.

teach.why: Shopify's hosted checkout keeps card data out of your build: Shopify is certified Level 1 PCI DSS and that covers stores on the platform. Handle card data anywhere else and PCI scope returns to the client, with a threat model mandatory.

options.pros: Card data never touches your code; Shopify's Level 1 PCI DSS compliance extends to the store
options.cons: Checkout changes are limited to Checkout Extensibility, and the deeper steps need Plus

options.pros: Keeps the client's acquirer and its card-data scope; no card data in your build
options.cons: Breaks the checkout journey; third-party transaction fees; local-currency charging is lost unless the provider is Adyen

options.pros: Full control of the payment experience
options.cons: Puts the client back in PCI scope, triggers a mandatory security review and threat model, and is a STOP for the standard offer

teach.limits: Shopify's certification covers the store, cart and hosting. It does not remove the merchant's own PCI obligations wherever they store, process or transmit cardholder data outside Shopify.

questions.text: Which express checkouts are required?
questions.help: B2B checkout and pre-orders do not support express checkouts.

teach.why: Express wallets are the strongest single conversion lever at checkout, but they are not universal: B2B checkout and pre-orders do not support them. Confirm this before promising one-tap buying to a trade audience or a pre-order launch.
teach.limits: B2B checkout and pre-orders do not support express checkouts.

questions.text: Must payment methods be hidden, renamed or reordered by market, customer type or cart?
questions.help: Needs a payment customization app (Shopify Function).

extension_points: Payment Customization Function (public apps: all plans; custom apps: Plus)

teach.why: Hiding, renaming or reordering payment methods is not a setting. It is a Payment Customization Shopify Function, so it means an app. A public app carrying that Function installs on any plan; the same Function inside a custom app needs Plus.
teach.limits: Public apps from the App Store containing Shopify Functions install on any plan. A custom app containing a Function requires Plus - that distinction, not the rule itself, decides the plan.

questions.text: Which checkout changes are needed?
questions.help: Shopify checkout is customised with the checkout editor and Checkout Extensibility (blocks, fields, logic via Functions). A fully custom checkout UI is not possible on Shopify.

native.feature: Checkout and accounts editor; Thank you / Order status page extensions
Checkout UI extensions on information, shipping and payment steps; Checkout Branding API

extension_points: Shopify Functions (public apps: all plans; custom apps: Plus)

teach.why: This is the plan question in disguise. Thank-you and order-status extensions run on every plan; anything touching the information, shipping or payment steps, or restyling through the Checkout Branding API, is Plus. A fully custom checkout UI is not possible at all.
teach.limits: checkout.liquid is retired - Checkout Extensibility (blocks, fields, Functions) is the only route, so a bespoke checkout front end is a STOP and a composable-platform conversation, not an estimate.

questions.text: Which checkout extensions are needed?

native.plan_note: Step extensions: Plus

teach.why: Names the actual extension points so the work is estimable: UI extensions for what the buyer sees, and Functions for delivery options, payment rules, cart and checkout validation and pickup points. Each Function is an app to build, review and maintain.
teach.limits: Checkout UI extensions run from Basic, but extensions on the information, shipping and payment steps are Plus. Functions inside a custom app are Plus; inside a public App Store app they are not.

questions.text: Which custom checkout fields are needed (company, VAT number, PO number, delivery instructions)?

teach.why: Extra fields - company, VAT number, PO number, delivery instructions - are checkout UI extensions, so where they sit decides the plan: on the information, shipping or payment steps they are Plus, on the thank-you page they are not.
teach.limits: Each field also needs a destination downstream; capturing it at checkout is only half the requirement if the ERP or invoicing system must receive it.

questions.text: Are post-purchase upsells needed?
questions.help: Upsells on the Thank you page are native; a separate post-purchase page is a Shopify beta.

native.plan_note: Post-purchase page: beta

teach.why: Upsells after payment are the cheapest incremental revenue in checkout and, unlike changes to the checkout steps, do not need Plus. Thank-you page extensions run from Basic; the separate post-purchase page is still a Shopify beta.
teach.limits: Thank-you page upsell extensions: Basic and above. A separate post-purchase page is in beta - treat it as a risk, not a commitment.

questions.text: Is store credit needed?
questions.help: Store credit is native: refund to store credit or issue credit; customers spend it when signed in.

teach.why: Removes a common assumption that this needs an app. Shopify can refund to store credit or issue it outright, and customers spend it when signed in - which quietly makes customer accounts part of the journey you design.
teach.limits: Customers must be signed in to spend store credit.

questions.text: Is manual fraud review needed for high-value orders?
questions.help: Native: fraud analysis and the Shopify Fraud Control app.

teach.why: Fraud review is native, but availability depends on the payment set-up as much as the plan. Fraud analysis covers Shopify Payments stores, and Grow, Advanced or Plus stores on most third-party processors, so a Basic store on a third-party gateway has none.
teach.limits: Fraud analysis: Shopify Payments stores, or Grow, Advanced and Plus stores on most third-party processors.

questions.text: Which order restrictions are needed?
questions.help: Blocking countries is native (markets and shipping zones); other rules need a cart and checkout validation app (Shopify Function).

teach.why: Splits the answer into free and paid. Blocking whole countries is native through markets and shipping zones; anything conditional - order value, quantity, product mix, customer type - is a Cart and Checkout Validation Function, which means an app.
teach.limits: A validation Function in a public App Store app works on any plan; the same Function in a custom app requires Plus.

questions.text: Do you want a guarantee that fraud chargebacks are reimbursed?
questions.help: Outside Shopify Protect (US Shop Pay orders) this needs a fraud app.

native.plan_note: US merchants, Shop Pay orders

teach.why: A reimbursement guarantee is rarely native. Shopify Protect requires a US-located merchant with a US Shopify Payments account and covers only Shop Pay orders of physical goods, so in Europe this is always a paid fraud app.
teach.limits: Shopify Protect also requires fulfilment with valid tracking within 7 days and the order in transit within 10 days. Treat it as a US-only benefit in European scoping.

questions.text: Do you fulfil in-house, through a 3PL, or both?

teach.why: Decides who owns fulfilment in the build: Shopify locations worked in the admin, or a 3PL connector with its own order, inventory and tracking sync. It sets the integration effort, the go-live cutover and who handles exceptions.

questions.text: Which 3PL provider?

teach.why: The named provider decides whether a ready-made Shopify connector exists or the integration has to be built and tested. It also fixes what flows back — stock levels, tracking numbers, returns — and the error handling you have to scope.

questions.text: How many locations will fulfil online orders (warehouses, 3PL locations and stores that ship orders), and in which countries are they?
questions.help: Physical stores that sell in person are counted separately in § 5.6.

native.plan_note: 10 locations below Plus, 200 on Plus; app locations not counted

teach.why: Location count sets both plan and routing scope. Shopify allows 10 locations below Plus and 200 on Plus. More than two fulfilling locations with routing beyond the native rules triggers a multi-location inventory scoping exercise.
teach.limits: 10 inventory locations on Basic, Grow and Advanced; 200 on Plus. Locations created by apps are not counted.

questions.why_it_matters: Where stock sits decides what a customer pays at the border, which tax schemes are open to you, and whether a country can be served from the same store as the others or needs its own operation.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A count and the country of each location, including 3PL sites. "Three warehouses" without countries is not usable — ask which countries they are in.

unknown_path.fallback: Locations are assumed to sit in the headquarters country (Q1.1.2), which keeps cross-border duties and the tax position as they are today.
unknown_path.assumption: All fulfilment happens from the home country.
unknown_path.resolve_by: A list of warehouse and 3PL sites from operations.

questions.text: How should Shopify pick the fulfilling location?
questions.help: Shopify's order routing rules: minimise split shipments, stay within the market, closest location, ranked locations, location metafields. Anything else needs a custom routing function or the ERP / OMS.

teach.why: Shopify picks a location with native routing rules: minimise split shipments, stay within the market, closest location, ranked locations, location metafields. Anything else means a custom routing Function or the ERP deciding — a different, larger build.

options.pros: Available from Basic, configured in the admin, no code, changeable by the client later.
options.cons: Only the documented strategies; no bespoke logic such as capacity, cost or carrier cut-off times.

options.option: Custom Order Routing Location Rule Function, or the ERP/OMS decides
options.pros: Any routing logic the business actually uses; fits clients whose OMS is already the source of truth.
options.cons: Development and ongoing maintenance, and it triggers the multi-location inventory scoping flag (T3).

questions.text: Which carriers do you use?

teach.why: The carrier list tells you which rates, labels and tracking can live inside Shopify and which stay in the carrier's own system or need an app. It is also the first input to the shipping-rate and label decisions below.

questions.text: How are shipping rates calculated?
questions.help: Flat, weight or price based, free above a threshold, live carrier rates, or rates from an app.

native.plan_note: Add-on on Grow

teach.why: Flat, weight-based and price-based rates are native from Basic. Live third-party carrier-calculated rates need Advanced or Plus, and on Grow only as a paid add-on or with annual billing. This answer can move the plan and the price.

options.option: Native rate tables (flat, weight, price conditions)
options.pros: Works from Basic, no extra cost, fully configurable by the client.
options.cons: Rates are your own estimates, so margin drifts when carrier pricing changes.

options.pros: Checkout shows the carrier's real price for the basket and destination.
options.cons: Needs Advanced or Plus (extra fee or annual billing on Grow), a carrier account, and accurate weights and package sizes.

teach.limits: Third-party carrier-calculated shipping is available on Advanced and Plus; Grow stores can add it for an extra monthly fee or by switching to annual billing.

questions.text: Are there product-specific shipping rules (heavy, hazardous, temperature-controlled)?

teach.why: Heavy, hazardous or temperature-controlled products normally need their own delivery profile, their own rates and a separate carrier arrangement. Missed at discovery, they appear after launch as rates that quote impossible deliveries.

questions.text: Which countries do you not ship to?

teach.why: Shipping zones and market setup are built from where you will not ship. Get it wrong and customers reach checkout for destinations you cannot serve, which comes back as cancellations, refunds and support load.

questions.text: Free-shipping thresholds per market (market, threshold, currency, which rates).
questions.help: Native: a rate condition based on order price, or an automatic free-shipping discount.

native.feature: Free-shipping rate condition or automatic free-shipping discount

teach.why: Free shipping is native either as a price condition on a shipping rate or as an automatic free-shipping discount. Thresholds that differ by market and currency multiply the rates and discounts to configure and test — effort, not development.
teach.limits: Both mechanisms are native from Basic; the cost is per-market configuration and testing.

questions.text: Which delivery methods do you offer?
questions.help: Local delivery and pickup in store are native. Pickup points are native only for stores in France, Italy, Spain and the UK (with some carriers); elsewhere they need a delivery app or a custom solution. Delivery time slots need an app; ship from store needs Shopify POS.

native.feature: Pickup points (native carriers in France, Italy, Spain, UK)
native.plan_note: Elsewhere: custom app with the pickup point Function on Plus; not for B2B or express wallets

teach.why: Local delivery and pickup in store are native. Pickup points are native only for stores in France, Italy, Spain and the UK with certain carriers. Delivery time slots need an app; ship from store needs Shopify POS.
teach.limits: Outside France, Italy, Spain and the UK, pickup points need a custom app using the Pickup Point Delivery Option Generator Function on Plus, and are not available for B2B or express wallets.

questions.text: How are shipping labels created?

teach.why: Where labels are created decides where tracking numbers come from, and therefore whether customers get shipping notifications automatically or someone has to type numbers back into Shopify. It also decides which team works in the admin daily.

options.pros: Tracking and fulfilment status update automatically; one place for the operations team to work.
options.cons: Needs accurate weights and a default package, and label support depends on the carrier and country.

options.option: Labels from the carrier's or 3PL's system
options.pros: Keeps existing carrier contracts, rates and warehouse processes untouched.
options.cons: Tracking numbers must be written back to Shopify by integration, or notifications and the order status page go stale.

questions.text: Do all products have accurate weights (and package sizes), and where does that data come from?
questions.help: Weight-based and carrier-calculated rates, shipping labels and some duties calculations need product weights.

native.plan_note: Labels need accurate weights and a default package

teach.why: Weight-based rates, carrier-calculated rates, shipping labels and some duty calculations all read product weights and packages. Missing or inherited-from-the-old-platform weight data is a migration task, and it breaks rates quietly after launch.
teach.limits: Labels need accurate weights and a default package configured.

questions.text: Do any products count as dangerous goods for shipping?
questions.help: E.g. aerosols (sprays, some sunscreens), flammable liquids (perfumes, alcohol-based products), lithium batteries, dry ice. They usually need their own delivery profile and carrier arrangements.

native.feature: Shipping dangerous goods (merchant responsibility; restricted with Shopify Shipping labels)
native.plan_note: USPS and FedEx labels bought in Shopify don't support hazardous materials

teach.why: Dangerous goods stay the merchant's responsibility and restrict what Shopify can do: USPS and FedEx labels bought inside Shopify do not support hazardous materials. These products need their own delivery profile and a direct carrier arrangement.
teach.limits: USPS and FedEx labels bought through Shopify do not support hazardous materials.

questions.text: Does a single order ever need to go to more than one address — gifts to several recipients, or one wholesale order split across branches?
questions.help: Different from an order arriving in several parcels, which Shopify does on its own.

teach.why: Shopify cannot deliver one order to more than one address. Asked late, it becomes a change request in UAT; asked now, the answer is one order per address, an app, or dropping it — and all three are cheaper than discovering it.
teach.limits: Split shipping divides an order into several shipments when items cannot travel together — a preorder line, a subscription, stock in different locations, different shipping profiles — and the customer picks a shipping option per shipment. Every shipment still goes to one address, the customer cannot choose how the order splits, and split shipping does not apply to accelerated checkouts or to draft orders that already carry a shipping line.

questions.text: Summarise the returns policy (window, conditions, who pays return postage).

teach.why: The written policy is exactly what you configure as return rules — window, return fee, restocking fee, final sale — or what a returns app must reproduce. Capturing it early shows whether the native rules can express it at all.

questions.text: Shopify includes return requests in customer accounts, controlled by return rules (window, return fee, restocking fee, final sale). Is that enough?

teach.why: This is the question that settles the returns line in the proposal: native self-serve returns and return rules, or a paid returns platform. Everything else in this subsection is evidence feeding this single decision.

options.option: Native self-serve returns and return rules
options.pros: Included from Basic, no licence, one system for staff, works for B2B orders too.
options.cons: Staff approve and handle exchanges manually; no QR drop-off; labels only for US locations.

options.pros: Customer-chosen exchanges and store credit, labels and QR drop-off outside the US, return reasons and reporting, automation at volume.
options.cons: Recurring licence cost, another system for staff and support, and an integration to keep in step.

teach.limits: Native return rules cover window, return fee, restocking fee and final sale. Return labels are only bought for US fulfilment locations, and customers cannot choose an exchange in the return form.

questions.text: Do you process exchanges (not only refunds)?

teach.why: Exchanges exist natively only as items staff add when approving a return — the customer never picks the replacement. A yes here is usually the first hard signal that a returns platform belongs in the recommendation.

questions.text: Which returns, tracking or post-purchase apps do you use or prefer?

teach.why: An incumbent returns or tracking platform turns the recommendation from choosing a tool into integrating one, with its own contract, data and migration. Ask before the app shortlist is drafted, not after the client sees it.

questions.text: How many days do customers have to return an order?

teach.why: The window is a native return rule, so the number itself is configuration. It matters here because unusual windows, or windows that change by market or product, are what push the client past what one native rule set can express.

questions.text: What share of orders is returned today (%)?
questions.help: High return rates or volumes usually justify a returns platform instead of Shopify's native self-serve returns.

teach.why: Return volume is the commercial test for a returns platform: at a high rate, approving every return by hand in the admin becomes a staffing cost. This number is what justifies — or rules out — the app licence in the final document.

questions.text: How do customers send items back: prepaid label, QR code drop-off, their own shipment, or mixed?
questions.help: Shopify creates return labels only for US fulfilment locations; other countries, or QR drop-off, need a returns app.

native.plan_note: US fulfilment locations only

teach.why: Shopify buys return labels only for US fulfilment locations, and QR-code drop-off is not native at all. For a European or cross-border client, prepaid labels or QR drop-off mean a returns app — this question exists to detect that.

options.option: Customer arranges and pays for their own shipment
options.pros: No label infrastructure needed; native returns are enough; no app licence.
options.cons: Worse customer experience, more support contact, and no tracking of inbound parcels.

options.pros: Expected by consumers, gives inbound tracking and lets refunds be triggered on carrier scan.
options.cons: Outside US fulfilment locations this needs a returns app plus a carrier account, both recurring costs.

teach.limits: Native return labels are limited to US fulfilment locations.

questions.text: Who pays return shipping: you, the customer, or it depends on the market?

teach.why: Who pays decides whether a return fee belongs in the rules and whether labels have to be bought at all. An answer of "it depends on the market" is the point where one native rule set stops being enough.

questions.text: Which exchanges do you offer: same product in another variant, any other product, or store credit first?
questions.help: Customers can't choose an exchange in Shopify's return form; staff add exchange items when approving. Customer-chosen exchanges need an app.

native.feature: Exchanges added by staff on return approval

teach.why: Customers cannot choose an exchange in Shopify's return form; staff add exchange items when approving. Variant swaps, any-product exchanges and store-credit-first flows are app features, so any answer other than "none" is an app signal.

questions.text: Do you accept international returns (including refunding duties)?

native.feature: Returns and duties refunds for international orders
native.plan_note: Native return labels only for US locations

teach.why: Returns and duty refunds for international orders are handled natively, but the return label is not — Shopify buys those only for US fulfilment locations. Cross-border returns therefore usually add a returns app plus carrier paperwork.
teach.limits: Native return labels only for US fulfilment locations.

questions.text: Must returned items be inspected before the refund or exchange is issued?

teach.why: Inspection puts a manual step between the parcel arriving and the money moving. It sets the refund trigger, who performs the check, where the result is recorded, and how long the customer waits — process and staffing as much as system.

questions.text: Do you need to capture and report return reasons?

teach.why: Reason capture is what turns returns into merchandising and quality data. Ask where the reporting must live — the Shopify admin, a returns app or the client's BI stack — because that is what decides whether a platform is needed.

questions.text: Should B2B customers request returns online (if you sell B2B)?
questions.help: Shopify's return requests also work for B2B orders.

teach.why: Shopify's return requests also work for B2B orders, so this is usually configuration rather than a build. It matters because B2B return approval and credit handling often sit in the ERP, and that part is integration work.

questions.text: Do return windows or conditions differ by market or product (e.g. final-sale items)?
questions.help: Final sale per product or collection is native.

teach.why: Final sale is native per product or collection. Windows or conditions that vary by market are where a single native rule set runs out and a returns platform enters scope. This is a deliberate detector question.

questions.text: Do order, shipping and delivery notifications need custom design or content?
questions.help: Shopify notifications are editable; SMS shipping notifications are native.

teach.why: Shopify's notification templates are editable and SMS shipping notifications are native. The answer decides whether this is template work in the admin, or a reason to send from the client's email platform instead.

questions.text: Are notifications sent by Shopify, by the email platform, or both?

teach.why: Who sends decides the integration and who owns the content after go-live. Splitting between Shopify and the email platform also creates the duplicate-message risk, so agree the split per notification, not in principle.

options.pros: No integration, order data is always current, SMS shipping notifications included.
options.cons: Template and design control is limited to what the notification editor allows, and reporting sits apart from the marketing stack.

options.pros: One brand template set and one reporting view across marketing and transactional mail.
options.cons: Needs order events pushed to the platform, Shopify templates switched off carefully, and deliverability owned elsewhere.

questions.text: Should customers be able to cancel orders themselves?
questions.help: Customers can request cancellation of unshipped orders in their account; you approve. Instant cancellation without approval needs an app.

native.plan_note: Requests need merchant approval

teach.why: Customers can request cancellation of an unshipped order in their account, but a merchant must approve each request. If the client expects the order to disappear immediately, that is an app, not configuration.

options.pros: Included from Basic, keeps a human check before stock and money move.
options.cons: Not instant; someone must action every request, which is support effort at volume.

options.pros: Instant self-service cancellation and edits, fewer support contacts.
options.cons: Recurring licence, and it must be aligned with fulfilment cut-offs so cancelled orders are not already picked.

teach.limits: Native cancellation requests always need merchant approval.

questions.text: Until when can an order be cancelled?

teach.why: The cut-off has to match how quickly fulfilment picks orders, which with a 3PL can be minutes. It decides the rule you set, what support does with late requests, and whether "cancel" really means "refuse delivery".

questions.text: Do you allow partial cancellations (some items of an order)?

teach.why: Cancelling part of an order touches the refund calculation, restocking and the message sent to the warehouse or 3PL. The answer tells you whether cancellation is one simple rule or a case-by-case admin process with integration behind it.

questions.text: Should customers be able to edit an order after placing it (address, items)?
questions.help: Staff can edit orders natively; customers editing their own orders needs an app.

teach.why: Staff can edit orders natively; customers editing their own order after checkout cannot. A yes here means an order-editing app, so treat this as an app detector rather than a configuration question.
teach.limits: Native order editing is a staff action in the admin only.

questions.text: How are refunds paid: to the original payment method, as store credit, or as a gift card?

teach.why: The refund method decides the finance trail: original payment method, store credit and gift cards each land differently in reconciliation and in the ERP feed. Store credit also changes what customer accounts must show.

questions.text: When is a refund issued: on request, when the carrier scans the return, on receipt, or after inspection?
questions.help: Refunds on carrier scan need a returns platform connected to carrier tracking.

native.feature: Refunds on return approval or receipt

teach.why: Refunding on request, on approval or on receipt is native. Refunding when the carrier scans the parcel needs a returns platform wired to carrier tracking — a clean single-answer app signal, and one clients ask for without knowing the cost.

options.option: Refund on approval or on receipt (native)
options.pros: No app, and the money only moves once you hold the goods.
options.cons: Customer waits for transit plus handling, which drives "where is my refund" contacts.

options.pros: Fast refund, measurably better returns experience.
options.cons: Needs a returns platform connected to carrier tracking, and the client carries the risk on parcels that never arrive.

questions.text: Is the original shipping cost refunded: always, only when you are at fault, or never?

teach.why: Whether outbound shipping comes back changes the refund calculation on every single return and the wording of the policy. It is a common dispute, so pin down the "only when we are at fault" case explicitly rather than in principle.

questions.text: Do you charge a restocking fee?
questions.help: A restocking fee is a native return rule (percentage of the return).

teach.why: A restocking fee is a native return rule, expressed as a percentage of the return, so a yes costs configuration rather than development. It still needs checking against consumer law in each market the client sells to.

questions.text: Do you issue partial refunds (e.g. damaged or missing parts)?

teach.why: Partial refunds for damage or missing parts are a manual judgement call. The real question is who may issue one, up to what value, and how it reaches finance — permissions and process, not platform capability.

questions.text: Must refunds be approved by someone before they are paid?

teach.why: An approval step decides who holds refund permissions, how long the customer waits, and whether a returns tool has to model an approval queue at all. It is also the first control the client's finance team will ask about.

questions.text: Must cancellations and refunds be passed to your ERP or finance system?

teach.why: Cancellations and refunds are the hardest events to keep consistent between Shopify and finance, because money has already moved. A yes adds integration work, failure handling and reconciliation testing — not just one more webhook.

questions.text: Must cancellations be instant, without your approval?

teach.why: This question exists purely to detect an app. Shopify's cancellation requests always need merchant approval, so "instant, no approval" cannot be delivered by configuration — it needs an order editing and cancellation app.
teach.limits: Native cancellation requests need merchant approval; there is no native instant self-cancellation.

questions.text: Do you want a branded order-tracking page on your own site?
questions.help: Shopify includes an order status page and shipping emails. A branded tracking page, proactive carrier alerts or delivery estimates usually need a post-purchase app.

native.feature: Order status page and shipping notifications

teach.why: Shopify gives an order status page and shipping notifications, not a branded tracking page on the client's own site. A yes is the main trigger for a post-purchase tracking app, so establish what "branded" actually has to include.

options.option: Native order status page and shipping emails
options.pros: Included, no app, always in step with the order.
options.cons: Limited branding, no carrier-event alerts, and traffic that a tracking page would capture goes to the carrier's site.

options.pros: Branded tracking on your domain, proactive delay alerts, a merchandising surface after purchase.
options.cons: Recurring licence, another vendor holding order and address data, and theme work to embed it.

questions.text: On which channels should customers get proactive delivery updates (delays, out for delivery)?

teach.why: Email and SMS shipping notifications are native. Proactive delay and out-for-delivery alerts come from a platform reading carrier events, so the channel list here is what decides whether a tracking app is in the recommendation.

questions.text: Should product pages or checkout show estimated delivery dates?
questions.help: Shopify can show delivery dates at checkout: manual dates everywhere, automatic dates only for US fulfilment locations.

native.plan_note: Automatic dates: US fulfilment locations only

teach.why: Shopify can show delivery dates at checkout: manual dates anywhere, automatic dates only for US fulfilment locations. Outside the US, automatic estimates or dates on product pages need an app — a documented limit that decides this line item.

options.pros: Native, free, available wherever the client fulfils from.
options.cons: Static promises someone must maintain; no product-page estimate; no adjustment for real carrier performance.

options.pros: Estimates on product pages and checkout outside the US, tuned per product and destination.
options.cons: Licence cost, theme integration, and the estimate is only as good as the data the client feeds it.

teach.limits: Automatic delivery dates are limited to US fulfilment locations; elsewhere dates at checkout are set manually.

questions.text: Do customers need to open warranty, repair or servicing claims online?

teach.why: Warranty, repair and servicing claims have no native Shopify flow. A yes means an app or a custom build plus an operational process behind it, so scope it as its own item rather than folding it into returns.

questions.text: How many physical retail stores (including pop-ups) will sell with Shopify?
questions.help: 0 if none.

teach.why: Store count turns on the Retail and POS scope modifier and sizes the roll-out. More than five stores is quoted as a programme delivered in increments, or as a rate-carded run team — not as one project with one go-live.

questions.text: Point of sale at launch?

teach.why: Shopify POS and a third-party POS integrated to Shopify are very different builds: one is configuration, hardware and training; the other is an inventory, order and payment integration. This answer sets the whole retail workstream.

options.pros: One product catalogue, one inventory and one customer record across online and store; omnichannel services available natively.
options.cons: Hardware, staff retraining and a POS Pro subscription per location for the omnichannel services.

options.option: Existing third-party POS integrated to Shopify
options.pros: No change for store staff, keeps the incumbent retail contract and back-office reporting.
options.cons: Inventory and order sync to build and monitor; native omnichannel services such as ship from store do not apply.

questions.text: Which omnichannel services are needed in store?
questions.help: Pickup in store, ship from store, in-store returns of online orders, endless aisle, stock transfers, retail prices.

native.plan_note: POS Pro subscription per location; retail market catalogs need POS Pro or Plus

teach.why: The in-store services listed here come with POS Pro, which is a subscription per location — a recurring cost the client carries, not a one-off build. Retail market catalogs need POS Pro or Plus. Flag both before the price is agreed.
teach.limits: POS Pro is charged per location; retail market catalogs require POS Pro or Plus.

questions.text: In which countries are the stores?

teach.why: Store countries decide the payment, tax and hardware set-up each store needs and whether retail sits inside an existing market. Confirm them: POS hardware and retail payment availability are country-specific and must be checked per country.

questions.text: Is guest checkout the default, are accounts optional, or is registration required?

teach.why: This sets the login model for the whole storefront: whether a shopper can buy without an account. It also meets B2B — a B2B buyer must sign in with a customer account and be attached to a company location before contracted pricing applies.

options.pros: Fewest steps to a first order; nothing to migrate on day one.
options.cons: No account area, so order history, buy again, returns and store credit have nowhere to live.

options.pros: Guests still convert, and registered customers get the native account area (order history, buy again, returns, store credit).
options.cons: Two journeys to design, test and support; account adoption has to be earned.

options.pros: Every order is attached to a customer record — which is how B2B has to work anyway.
options.cons: A barrier in front of the first retail purchase.

questions.text: What should the account area include (order history, addresses, returns, wishlist, subscriptions)?

native.feature: Customer accounts (order history, buy again, returns, store credit)

teach.why: Order history, buy again, returns and store credit are native in customer accounts on every plan from Basic. Wishlists are not — they need an app. Anything beyond the native list is built as customer account UI extensions, so list the wanted features precisely.
teach.limits: Wishlist is an app decision: a vendor, a monthly cost and storefront integration, not a setting.

questions.text: How should customers sign in?
questions.help: One-time email code and Google or Facebook sign-in are native.

native.plan_note: Not compatible with the Customer Account API used by headless

teach.why: Shopify's current customer accounts sign in with a one-time email code, plus Google or Facebook — no password. Signing in from another site uses Multipass, which is Plus and is not compatible with the Customer Account API a headless storefront uses.
teach.limits: Legacy customer accounts (password-based) are the older generation: B2B does not support them, and headless customer accounts require the auth code to be moved off them.

questions.text: Do B2B customers need company accounts with their own login?

teach.why: This turns on Shopify's B2B model: companies, company locations, and buyers who sign in with customer accounts. It opens the B2B scope gate — and note that most of B2B runs on every plan from Basic, not only Plus.
teach.limits: A B2B order must be placed by a buyer associated with a company location; without that association D2C rates apply. Legacy customer accounts are not supported, so customer accounts must be activated first.

questions.text: Do B2B customers get company-specific price lists?
questions.help: Business price lists are B2B catalogs.

native.plan_note: Up to 3 active catalogs below Plus

teach.why: B2B price lists are catalogs. Below Plus you get up to three active catalogs and none can be assigned directly to a named company — company-specific pricing is the single most common reason a B2B project needs Plus. Confirm which they mean.
teach.limits: B2B catalogs on Basic, Grow and Advanced require the store to be on new Shopify Markets. Even on Plus, a company location can hold at most 25 catalogs.

questions.text: Are there B2B volume discounts or quantity rules?

teach.why: Quantity price breaks and quantity rules are native B2B on every plan from Basic, so a wholesale pricing ladder rarely needs an app. The answer also trips the B2B scope gate, which is what sizes the engagement.

questions.text: Which payment terms are needed (net 30, invoice, purchase order)?

native.feature: B2B payment terms, vaulted cards, draft orders
Deposits, partial payments, payment requests per fulfilment

teach.why: Net terms (Net 7 to Net 90), PO numbers, vaulted cards and draft orders are native from Basic. Deposits, partial payments and payment requests per fulfilment are Plus. One answer here can force a plan upgrade, so pin down exactly which terms.
teach.limits: B2B checkout does not support accelerated checkouts — Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Amazon Pay.

questions.text: Is there a request-for-quote workflow, or is pricing negotiated per buyer?
questions.help: Shopify has no built-in request-for-quote: orders can be submitted for review as drafts, or a quote app handles negotiation.

native.feature: Orders submitted for review as drafts

teach.why: Shopify has no built-in request-for-quote. Natively the nearest thing is requiring B2B orders to be placed as drafts, reviewed and edited by staff before confirmation. Anything resembling real negotiation needs a quote app — either way this flags a B2B architecture review.

options.pros: No extra vendor; works from Basic; can be required per company location and keeps one source of pricing truth.
options.cons: It is a review-and-edit step, not a quote document with a negotiation trail.

options.option: A quote app (App Store category "Pricing quotes")
options.pros: Covers quote request, negotiation and quote-to-order as a product feature.
options.cons: Adds a vendor dependency and a second source of pricing truth; the capability is not documented by Shopify and must be evidenced per app.

questions.text: Must B2B accounts be approved before they can order?
questions.help: Native: a wholesale application form (Shopify Forms) plus Flow to create and approve companies.

native.feature: Shopify Forms and Shopify Flow for company approval

teach.why: B2B access is granted by the merchant: a buyer only becomes a B2B buyer once staff attach them to a company location. Natively, a company account request form (free Shopify Forms app) collects applications and Shopify Flow automates the approval steps.
teach.limits: Inside a company location there are two permission levels: ordering only (own orders), and location admin (all orders at the location, plus address updates).

questions.text: Native Shopify B2B or an app?

teach.why: The architecture fork for B2B. Shopify publishes no comparison of the three routes, so decide it against two things we can evidence: the documented gaps in native B2B, and the plan the catalog model actually needs.

options.pros: One product and inventory source; companies, locations, net terms, PO numbers and price breaks on all plans; no third-party data processor.
options.cons: Documented gaps: no accelerated checkout, subscriptions, local delivery, pickup points or tipping; several features off by default; catalogs capped at three below Plus.

options.pros: Full separation of catalogue, theme and checkout; on Plus it can be an expansion store on the same contract.
options.cons: Two stores to build and run; stores in an organisation do not share data by default, and expansion stores are a Plus contract feature.

options.pros: Can cover documented gaps — for example payment-method restriction, which Shopify points to apps or the Payment Customization Function API for.
options.cons: Vendor dependency and a second source of pricing truth; app capability is not documented by Shopify and must be evidenced per app.

questions.text: How many B2B accounts are expected within 12 months?

teach.why: Volume sets the effort: how many companies and locations have to be created, imported and kept in step with the client's systems, and how many distinct price lists the model really needs — which is where the three-catalog limit below Plus starts to bite.
teach.limits: A company can have up to 10,000 company locations; each company location can have at most 25 catalogs assigned.

questions.text: How many distinct B2B price lists (catalogs) do you need, and must any be specific to one company?

native.plan_note: Up to 3 active catalogs below Plus

teach.why: The clearest plan test in B2B. Below Plus you get up to three active catalogs across all B2B markets, and none can be assigned directly to a company or location. More than three, or company-specific pricing, means Plus.
teach.limits: On Basic, Grow and Advanced the store must be on new Shopify Markets to use B2B catalogs at all.

questions.text: Should B2B buyers see a different storefront or checkout from consumers?

teach.why: A B2B-specific storefront and checkout is delivered through Markets, and customising the theme per market starts at Advanced. If buyers must see a different site from consumers, the plan floor moves up — establish that before quoting Basic or Grow.

questions.text: Do B2B orders need any of these: subscriptions, local delivery or pickup points, express checkouts, more than 500 line items, gift cards?
questions.help: Shopify B2B does not support these.

teach.why: The list of things Shopify B2B does not do at all: accelerated checkouts, subscriptions, local delivery, pickup points, tipping, and orders above 500 line items. A yes here is a flagged architecture review or a process change, never a configuration task.
teach.limits: Pickup in store, gift cards at checkout, line item scripts and abandoned checkouts are turned off by default for B2B and must be requested from Shopify Support by the store or organisation owner.

questions.text: Which shipping rules differ for B2B buyers?
questions.help: By default B2B and consumer buyers see the same shipping methods. Different options need Checkout Blocks, an app or a delivery customization function; orders can also be submitted as drafts so shipping is quoted before payment.

native.feature: B2B shipping methods (same as consumers by default; customise per buyer)
native.plan_note: Custom apps with Shopify Functions need Plus; public apps with functions work on any plan

native.feature: Submit B2B orders as drafts for review

teach.why: By default B2B buyers see the same shipping methods as consumers. Different options need Checkout Blocks, an app or a delivery customisation function — and a function inside a custom app needs Plus, while a public app containing one works on any plan.
teach.limits: Local delivery and pickup points are not supported in B2B. Where shipping must be quoted per order, B2B orders can be submitted as drafts and priced before payment.

questions.text: Is the wholesale side of the business run by its own team, with its own targets or its own profit and loss?
questions.help: We are asking about how the business is organised, not about the website.
questions.why_it_matters: A wholesale business with its own team, targets and customers usually wants to move at its own pace — its own campaigns, its own releases, its own data. That is the difference between wholesale living alongside the consumer store and wholesale having a store of its own.
questions.what_good_looks_like: A clear yes or no about the organisation. The follow-up that sharpens it: "who decides wholesale prices and campaigns, and do they report to the same person as ecommerce?"
questions.who_can_answer: Sales director, wholesale lead or the head of ecommerce.

unknown_path.fallback: Assumed false: wholesale is run by the same team as the consumer business, which keeps it on the same store.
unknown_path.resolve_by: One question to the commercial lead about who owns the wholesale number.

native.feature: B2B on one store: companies, locations and catalogs

teach.why: Native B2B runs on the same store as the consumer business, which is the cheaper answer whenever one team runs both. A separate wholesale team with its own P&L is the documented reason Shopify gives for an expansion store, so this answer is one of the criteria that moves the topology to a hybrid.
teach.limits: An expansion store needs Shopify Plus, and nothing is shared between stores — products, inventory, apps and themes are all maintained twice. Weigh it against keeping B2B on one store with its own catalogs.

questions.text: Which loyalty components are planned?
questions.help: Shopify has no native points programme; store credit can be a reward currency. Loyalty needs an app.

teach.why: Shopify has no native points programme, so loyalty means an app. What is native is store credit, which can serve as the reward currency and shows in the customer account. Naming the components now sizes the app choice and its integration work.

questions.text: Is loyalty needed at launch or in a later phase?

teach.why: Loyalty is an app plus integration and storefront work, not a toggle, so it belongs to a phase. Deciding launch or later stops it being quietly assumed into the first release and keeps the launch scope honest.
teach.limits: Store credit is native and can go live at launch even when the points programme comes later.

questions.text: Which loyalty app is used or preferred?

teach.why: If a loyalty app is already running, the job is migrating balances, tiers and history rather than selecting a vendor. If they only have a preference, it fixes the integration surface early. If neither, we shortlist from the App Store loyalty category.

questions.text: Must loyalty status sync to the email platform or CRM?

teach.why: Loyalty status living in the app while campaigns live in the email platform or CRM means a sync to build, monitor and keep correct. It is integration scope with its own failure modes, and it is where loyalty work usually overruns.

questions.text: Which customer segments do you use today?

teach.why: Today's segments show what customer data must arrive in Shopify and stay accurate. Shopify has native customer segments, so the list tells us what can be rebuilt natively and what depends on data another system holds.

questions.text: Where is segmentation driven from — Shopify, the email platform, a CDP, or a mix?
questions.help: Customer segments are native in Shopify; the email platform or CDP may own them instead.

teach.why: Segments can live natively in Shopify, in the email platform, or in a CDP. Where they live decides who owns the definitions, which system triggers campaigns, and which way customer data has to flow — and a mix means reconciling both.

options.pros: Native customer segments, no extra licence; they sit next to the order and customer data that define them.
options.cons: Any tool outside Shopify that needs the segment has to be fed by an integration.

options.option: The email platform or a CDP
options.pros: One definition across channels wider than the store, in a tool the client may already run.
options.cons: Shopify-side logic that keys off segments or tags — pricing, access, discounts — then has to be driven from outside.

options.pros: Each system keeps the segments it is genuinely best placed to own.
options.cons: Two sources of truth; the boundary has to be written down in the build, or it drifts.

questions.text: Which customer tags drive custom logic today (pricing, access, discounts)?

teach.why: Customer tags are usually load-bearing on the old platform — gating access, pricing or discounts. They have to be migrated and re-implemented here, and some of what tags did there is a B2B catalog or a customer segment in Shopify.

questions.text: Which privacy laws apply to your customers (GDPR, UK GDPR, CCPA, Swiss nFADP, other)?

teach.why: The regimes set the compliance baseline for everything else in this section: consent before tracking, opt-out pages, how data-subject requests are handled, and what legal must sign off. Ask it before the consent and data questions, not after.

questions.text: Cookie consent: Shopify's cookie banner or a consent management platform? Name the tool if known.
questions.help: Shopify's cookie banner is native; a third-party platform must integrate Shopify's Customer Privacy API.

teach.why: Whichever banner is used, the consent decision must reach Shopify through the Customer Privacy API — otherwise Shopify's own tracking and the installed apps never learn it. Shopify's native cookie banner does that already; a third-party platform has to be integrated.

options.pros: Native from Basic in the customer privacy settings, no licence, already wired into Shopify's consent handling.
options.cons: It covers this store only — no help if the client runs a group-wide consent record across other sites.

options.pros: One consent approach across the client's whole estate, often already contracted and owned by their legal team.
options.cons: It must integrate Shopify's Customer Privacy API — real delivery work and a testable requirement, plus the licence.

questions.text: Is explicit opt-in required for marketing emails?

teach.why: Explicit opt-in changes the sign-up forms, the checkout consent box and what the email platform may send. Get the answer in writing: it decides which of the collected addresses can actually be marketed to, at launch and after a migration.

questions.text: Do you collect sensitive personal data (health, age, biometric, financial)?
questions.help: Sensitive data needs a data protection impact assessment and legal sign-off.

teach.why: Special-category data (health, age, biometric, financial) raises the bar: a data protection impact assessment and legal sign-off on minimisation, storage location and consent before build. It is flagged early because it can reshape the data model and the timeline.

questions.text: Must data-access or deletion requests reach systems beyond Shopify (ERP, email platform) or run without staff involvement?
questions.help: Shopify handles export and erasure requests in admin; other systems or automation need extra design and legal sign-off.

teach.why: Shopify handles customer data export and erasure requests inside the admin. The moment a request must also reach the ERP, email platform or warehouse, or run without a person, it becomes a delivery workstream with legal sign-off — not a Shopify setting.
teach.limits: Every connected system that holds customer data widens the request: each one needs an owner, a route and evidence that it was done.

questions.text: Do US state privacy laws require a 'Do not sell or share my personal information' page?
questions.help: A native opt-out page honours Global Privacy Control.

teach.why: US state privacy laws can require a "Do not sell or share my personal information" page. Shopify's native opt-out page honours Global Privacy Control signals, so this is usually configuration rather than build — but it must be asked, decided and evidenced.

questions.text: Where do you collect marketing consent?

teach.why: Every point where consent is captured — newsletter form, checkout, account creation, pop-up, in store — is a point where the record must be created and carried. The list shows which integrations must write consent back, and where an audit would find gaps.

questions.text: Is organic search a significant traffic channel?

teach.why: If organic traffic carries the business, URL structure, redirects, metadata and page speed become build tasks with a budget rather than good intentions. If search is a minor channel, that effort is better spent elsewhere.

questions.text: Are custom URL structures needed?

teach.why: Tell us early if the brand depends on a particular URL pattern. What a platform can and cannot change has to be checked against the documentation before the content plan assumes it, and it sizes the redirect work on migration.

questions.text: Who manages SEO?

teach.why: SEO work does not stop at launch: redirects, metadata, structured data and content keep changing. This answer decides who holds that job and therefore whether we hand over an editable setup or carry the work ourselves.

options.option: Client or their SEO agency owns it
options.pros: Keeps specialist knowledge with the people who own the traffic targets; no ongoing cost in our scope
options.cons: The theme and the admin must be genuinely editable by a non-developer, and the handover and training become real deliverables

options.option: We own it as part of delivery
options.pros: One team accountable for the migration, the redirect map and the recovery of rankings
options.cons: Adds retained effort after launch, and someone on the client side still has to approve content and priorities

questions.text: Should products be discoverable in AI shopping assistants?
questions.help: Shopify Catalog and agentic channels (Spring '26).

teach.why: Shopify enrols eligible stores in agentic storefront channels by default, so doing nothing already answers this. The question confirms or reverses a channel that may be live now. Section 7.7 takes the decision apart in detail.
teach.limits: Eligibility is Shopify's: Starter plan or higher, store not in private mode, products with a title, an image, a price above zero and a published product URL. Business-only products are excluded automatically.

questions.text: Which analytics platforms do you use (GA4, Adobe, other)?

teach.why: Every analytics platform on Shopify is wired through the same event layer, but each needs its own setup, consent handling and test pass. The list sizes that work and tells us which numbers the client will judge the launch by.

questions.text: Is server-side tracking needed?
questions.help: Shopify's customer events track storefront and checkout with consent; the Facebook & Instagram and Google & YouTube apps send server-side events. Anything beyond needs a tracking app. Server-side events can share customer data with ad platforms (PII gate).

native.feature: Customer events (web pixels); Facebook & Instagram and Google & YouTube apps

teach.why: Shopify's customer events cover storefront and checkout with consent, and the Facebook & Instagram and Google & YouTube apps already send events server-side. Anything beyond that needs a tracking app or build work, and sharing customer data with ad platforms triggers the PII gate.

options.option: Stay with Shopify's customer events and the Meta and Google channel apps
options.pros: No extra licence, no extra integration, consent handled by the platform
options.cons: Limited to what those apps send; other ad or analytics destinations get browser-side data only

options.option: Add a server-side tracking app or a custom endpoint
options.pros: Better event delivery and matching for platforms Shopify's own apps do not cover
options.cons: Licence cost plus build and maintenance, and customer data leaving the store needs an explicit consent and PII decision

teach.limits: Native server-side sending is documented for the Facebook & Instagram and Google & YouTube apps; anything else is an app or a build item.

questions.text: Which advertising pixels are needed (Meta, TikTok, Pinterest, Google Ads)?

teach.why: Each advertising pixel is a separate install, a separate consent case and a separate test. The list decides how much tracking work the build carries and which conversion numbers marketing will reconcile after launch.

questions.text: Is a tag manager already configured?
questions.help: Tag managers run as a custom pixel in Shopify's sandbox; scripts in checkout are no longer possible.

teach.why: This matters more on Shopify than elsewhere: a tag manager runs as a custom pixel inside Shopify's sandbox, and scripts in checkout are no longer possible. An existing container has to be rebuilt to that model, not pasted across.

questions.text: Which custom events must be tracked beyond standard ecommerce events?

teach.why: Standard storefront and checkout events come from Shopify's customer events. Anything else — configurator steps, wishlist adds, quiz completions, store locator use — is code someone writes and tests in a pixel. Listing them now puts a price on them.

questions.text: Which email / CRM platform do you use or plan to use: Shopify Messaging or another platform (name)?
questions.help: Shopify Messaging covers email, SMS and WhatsApp campaigns and automations.

teach.why: Shopify Messaging covers email, SMS and WhatsApp campaigns and automations natively. A third-party platform has to earn its licence through segmentation, deeper flows and data that lives outside Shopify. This answer sets the integration work and the customer-data path.

options.pros: Native, no integration to build, customer data stays in Shopify, one place for email, SMS and WhatsApp
options.cons: Less sophisticated segmentation and flow logic than a dedicated platform; less useful if the CRM already lives elsewhere

options.pros: Richer segmentation, lifecycle flows and reporting; fits a brand whose customer data spans more than the store
options.cons: Licence cost, an integration to build and keep working, and customer data leaving Shopify — a PII decision, not just a technical one

questions.text: Which automated flows are needed (welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase, win-back)?

teach.why: Lifecycle flows are where recovered revenue comes from — abandoned cart above all. Each flow needs trigger data, content and a test pass, so the list sizes the marketing build and tells tracking which events it must actually produce.

questions.text: Do you send SMS marketing, and to which countries?

native.plan_note: AT, CA, DK, FI, IT, LU, PL, PT, SE, UK, US; Spain paused since 2026-09-15

teach.why: Shopify Messaging sends SMS only in a documented list of countries. Marketing by SMS outside that list means a third-party app, plus its own consent capture, sender registration and country rules — cost and legal work, not a switch.

options.pros: Native, no extra app, same place as email and WhatsApp campaigns
options.cons: Only the documented countries, so a multi-market brand can outgrow it mid-project

options.pros: Covers countries Shopify Messaging does not, usually with deeper automation
options.cons: Licence and per-message cost, an integration, and consent data held outside Shopify

teach.limits: Shopify Messaging SMS is documented for AT, CA, DK, FI, IT, LU, PL, PT, SE, UK and US; Spain has been paused since 15 September 2026.

questions.text: Do you send WhatsApp marketing?
questions.help: Native in Shopify Messaging.

teach.why: WhatsApp marketing is native in Shopify Messaging, so a yes may cost no extra tool — but it still needs opt-in capture, message templates and someone to run the channel. A no keeps it out of scope and out of the estimate.

questions.text: Which product reviews app is used or preferred?
questions.help: Product reviews need an app.

teach.why: Product reviews are not native on Shopify; they need an app. The choice decides where review content lives, how it is migrated from the current provider, how the theme renders stars and how much the licence costs each month.

questions.text: Is user-generated content important (customer photos, social embeds)?

teach.why: Customer photos and social walls are tool-plus-theme work: rights management, moderation, extra media on the product page and the page speed that comes with it. A yes adds a licence and template changes; a no keeps the page lean.

questions.text: Which affiliate platform, if any?

teach.why: An affiliate platform sits outside the store and needs feeding: order values, codes and attribution at the point of purchase. Naming it now tells us what has to be wired and reconciled, rather than discovering it when commissions do not match.

questions.text: Do you use Shopify Collabs for influencers?
questions.help: Shopify Collabs isn't accepting new creator sign-ups; you can still invite creators.

teach.why: Shopify Collabs is not accepting new creator sign-ups, though existing programmes can still invite creators. If the influencer plan assumed Collabs would recruit for the brand, that has to be re-planned during discovery, not after launch.

questions.text: Are affiliate and influencer sales tracked via discount codes, UTM parameters, or both?

teach.why: This decides how commission is calculated and which reports have to agree. Codes attribute the order but discount it and travel further than intended; UTMs attribute the session but break across devices. Most brands end up reconciling both.

options.pros: Attribution survives to the order and is visible in the store's own reporting; works offline and in video
options.cons: Every sale is discounted, codes get shared on voucher sites, and codes collide with other promotions and combination rules

options.pros: No margin given away, and the click is tied to a real campaign source
options.cons: Lost when the shopper switches device or buys later; needs analytics and consent to be working properly to count anything

questions.text: Which discount types are used?

teach.why: Each discount type is one of three things: an admin setting, a native combination, or a discount function someone writes and maintains. Listing the types is what tells us which — and that is the whole difference in cost.

questions.text: Which discounts must combine on one order?
questions.help: Shopify combines product, order and shipping discounts natively (up to 5 codes plus 1 shipping code, and up to 25 automatic discounts). Custom logic needs a discount function.

native.plan_note: Up to 5 codes + 1 shipping code; 25 automatic discounts

native.feature: Several product discounts on the same line item
native.plan_note: Plan requirement to recheck after Spring '26

teach.why: Stacking is where the promotion plan meets platform limits. Shopify combines product, order and shipping discounts natively; several product discounts on the same item is a Plus feature, and anything outside the native rules needs a discount function.

options.pros: Configuration only, no code to maintain, no plan change; merchandising can run promotions unaided
options.cons: The promotion calendar has to respect the documented limits and the combination rules

options.pros: Any bespoke rule the business wants, applied consistently in cart and checkout
options.cons: Development, testing and long-term ownership of code that touches every order's price

teach.limits: Up to 5 discount codes plus 1 shipping code on an order, and up to 25 automatic discounts. Several product discounts on the same line item requires Plus — a plan requirement to recheck after Spring '26.

questions.text: Are coupon codes single-use, multi-use, or bulk-generated?

teach.why: A handful of shared codes is admin configuration. Unique codes per customer, affiliate or gift are a generation, storage and reporting problem — usually an import or an app — and the volumes decide whether that is a small job or a real one.

options.pros: Created in the admin in minutes, easy to communicate and to report on
options.cons: Shared publicly the moment one customer posts it; no per-customer control

options.pros: One code per customer or partner, so misuse is contained and attribution is exact
options.cons: Needs generation, distribution and reporting to be built or licensed, and the volumes have to be planned

questions.text: Must codes be brand-named (e.g. WELCOME20)?

teach.why: Brand-named codes are memorable, which is the point and the risk: they are guessed, shared and posted to voucher sites. The answer tells us whether the promotion relies on secrecy, and therefore on usage limits and customer eligibility instead.

questions.text: Do codes need minimum order values or quantities?

teach.why: Thresholds are ordinary discount conditions, but they have to be agreed per market and currency by the business, and the storefront must tell the shopper how far off the threshold they are. That is configuration plus theme work plus testing.

questions.text: Do codes expire on a fixed date, a rolling period, or never?

teach.why: A fixed end date is a setting. A rolling period — thirty days from sign-up, say — means a code generated per customer by a flow or an app. The answer separates configuration from a small piece of engineering.

questions.text: How are codes distributed (email, SMS, print, influencers)?

teach.why: Where codes go decides who creates them and in what volume, whether the email or SMS platform has to generate them, and whether the store must honour codes it did not issue — print runs and influencer lists especially.

questions.text: Do promotions differ by market, customer segment, sales channel or B2B company?

teach.why: Targeting turns a promotion from a setting into a rules problem: who qualifies, in which market, channel and currency, and what the storefront shows everyone else. It is also where plan requirements appear, so it is asked early.
teach.limits: Per-market customisation is documented as an Advanced plan feature; company-specific catalogues or more than three B2B catalogues require Plus (exit rule 11.1).

questions.text: Are gift cards sold as a product?
questions.help: Gift cards are native: digital cards by email, physical cards on POS; they never expire by default. Also covers gift cards accepted at checkout.

teach.why: Gift cards are native — digital cards sent by email, physical cards through POS — and they never expire by default. So selling them is configuration, not a build; what needs work is the card design, the delivery email and the process behind them.

questions.text: Are gift cards issued as rewards or compensation?

teach.why: Issuing cards as goodwill or compensation is a service process, not a storefront one: who may issue, up to what value, with what approval, and how finance sees the outstanding liability. It also decides who needs admin access.

questions.text: Digital gift cards, physical, or both?

teach.why: These are two different projects. Digital cards are sent by email and are close to configuration. Physical cards are sold and activated through POS, which brings retail hardware, stock, in-store process and staff training into scope.

options.pros: Native delivery by email, no stock, no retail process, live quickly
options.cons: No product to put in a shop or a gift box; loses the in-store and last-minute gift occasion

options.pros: Sellable in store and as a gift object; supports retail and wholesale occasions
options.cons: Card production, stock, POS activation and staff process — a retail workstream, not a storefront setting

questions.text: Must gift cards expire?

teach.why: Gift cards never expire by default, so a yes is a deliberate change that has to be checked against the law in each market the brand sells in — and against how finance wants the balance treated. Ask before assuming either.

questions.text: Are promotions triggered from email or SMS campaigns?

teach.why: If a campaign platform triggers the promotion, someone has to create the matching codes or automatic discounts in Shopify and keep the two in step. That is an integration and a weekly operating routine, not a one-off setup.

questions.text: Does each campaign need its own landing page?

teach.why: A page per campaign is fine if marketing can build one from existing sections. If not, every campaign becomes a developer ticket. The answer shapes how flexible the theme has to be and how much handover training is needed.

questions.text: Are countdown timers or urgency elements needed?
questions.help: Countdown timers need an app or theme work.

teach.why: Countdown timers and urgency badges are not a setting: they need an app or theme work, and they touch page speed, caching and, in some markets, rules on pressure selling. Small, but a real build item with a real owner.

options.pros: Marketing can schedule and style timers without a developer
options.cons: Monthly licence, another script on the page, and the look is constrained by the app

options.pros: Exactly the brand's design, no licence, no third-party script
options.cons: Every new campaign format is a developer change, and caching has to be handled carefully

questions.text: Do you run scheduled drops or flash sales with high traffic?
questions.help: Scheduled theme and checkout changes are native (Rollouts).

teach.why: Drops squeeze a month of traffic and stock contention into minutes. Scheduling theme and checkout changes is native through Rollouts, on the Grow plan; the rest — stock rules, queueing, load testing, a rehearsal — is planning that must start early.
teach.limits: Rollouts (scheduled theme and checkout changes) is documented on the Grow plan.

questions.text: Do you want your products to be found and bought inside AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Google AI or Copilot?
questions.help: AI assistants are becoming a shopping channel. Shopify already switches eligible stores on by default, so this is a decision to confirm or reverse, not one to postpone.

native.feature: Agentic storefronts (active by default for eligible stores)

teach.why: This decides whether a new sales channel is open or closed. Shopify enrols eligible stores automatically, so doing nothing is itself a decision — the channel is on.

options.pros: Reaches shoppers who start in an assistant instead of a search engine; no build work — Shopify feeds the catalogue
options.cons: Less control over presentation; the assistant owns the conversation; customer data is shared when checkout happens inside it

options.pros: Full control of the journey and the data
options.cons: Invisible where a growing share of product research starts; competitors listed instead

teach.limits: Eligibility is decided by Shopify: Starter plan or higher, not a private store, and some channels only for merchants selling to US buyers. Business-to-business products are excluded automatically.

questions.text: Should Shopify enrol you automatically in new AI channels as they appear, or do you want to approve each one?
questions.help: The default setting also enrols you in channels that do not exist yet.

native.feature: Agentic channel management (Shopify-managed or per channel)

teach.why: AI channels are being added regularly. This decides whether the brand appears in a new one automatically, or only after your review.

options.pros: No admin work; the brand is present as new channels launch
options.cons: The brand can appear in a channel nobody reviewed, with terms and data sharing accepted in advance

options.pros: Brand, legal and data review before each launch
options.cons: Someone must own the review; the brand is late to new channels

teach.limits: The default is Shopify-managed enrolment, with catalogue access and checkout inside the assistant switched on.

questions.text: Should shoppers be able to pay inside the AI assistant, or should they come to your store to check out?
questions.help: Paying in the assistant converts better; sending them to your store keeps the full journey, the upsells and the analytics.

native.plan_note: Per channel; ChatGPT is referral only

teach.why: This is the commercial trade-off of the channel: conversion against ownership of the customer journey and the data.

options.pros: Fewer steps, so better conversion from an assistant conversation
options.cons: Your storefront, upsells and analytics are skipped; the channel receives the customer's name, e-mail, phone and address

options.pros: You keep merchandising, upsells, tracking and the customer relationship
options.cons: More steps between intent and purchase

teach.limits: ChatGPT always sends shoppers to your checkout; other channels can be set per channel.

questions.text: Do you sell to customers in the United States?
questions.help: Some AI channels are only open to merchants selling to US buyers, wherever the business is based.

native.plan_note: Starter plan or higher; some channels need US buyers

teach.why: It decides which AI channels are available at all, so it decides whether this section matters for launch.
teach.limits: ChatGPT and Copilot need US buyers; Google's AI channels are limited to selected US-based shops. A European merchant selling only in Europe may not be eligible today.

questions.text: Who can accept Shopify's additional terms for selling through AI channels?
questions.help: Selling through these channels requires accepting separate terms — usually legal or procurement, not the ecommerce team.

teach.why: The channel cannot go live until someone with authority accepts separate terms. Naming that person early avoids a launch-week block.
teach.limits: The supplemental terms are accepted in the Shopify admin, and acceptance covers the channels the store is enrolled in.

questions.text: Are you comfortable sharing the customer's name, e-mail, phone and address with an AI channel when they buy inside it?
questions.help: This is a data-protection decision. Under GDPR it usually needs a documented review before launch.

native.feature: Customer data shared with agentic channels on direct checkout

teach.why: Checkout inside the assistant means order data reaches a third party. It is the same kind of decision as adding a new processor, and it belongs with the data-protection owner.

options.pros: Checkout inside the assistant stays available, with its conversion benefit
options.cons: A third party processes customer data; needs a record and probably a contract

options.pros: No new processor; simpler privacy position
options.cons: Checkout in the assistant must be switched off; the channel becomes referral only

teach.limits: The data is shared only for orders placed through direct checkout in the channel.

questions.text: How complete is your product data — titles, images, prices, descriptions and variants?
questions.help: AI channels only list products whose data is complete. Gaps make products invisible rather than badly presented.

teach.why: Product-data quality decides visibility in AI channels, and it is the cheapest thing to fix before launch.
teach.limits: A product needs a title, at least one image, a price above zero, an identifiable URL and publication to the online store. Eligibility is reviewed over time, not only once.

questions.text: Is important product information kept in custom fields, separate records or inside the product title (for example “Steel 40mm — Automatic”)?
questions.help: Data that lives in custom fields or in the title needs mapping before AI channels can read it.

teach.why: It decides whether there is a data workstream. Attributes that matter commercially — material, size, movement — are often in custom fields or packed into titles, where an assistant cannot read them reliably.
teach.limits: Shopify supports mapping custom fields and title patterns into the catalogue it sends to AI channels; that mapping is work to plan.
