questions.text: Should AI crawlers be allowed, restricted or blocked on your website?
questions.help: Blocking crawlers does not remove your products from AI shopping channels; it only affects what they read from your public site.

teach.why: Brands often want to block AI crawlers to protect content, then find their products still appear — the two routes are separate.

options.pros: Editorial content, guides and brand story can be cited by assistants
options.cons: Content can be summarised without a visit to the site

options.pros: Protects editorial content and images from open-web crawling
options.cons: No effect on the product data Shopify sends to AI channels; can reduce visibility in AI answers

teach.limits: Crawler rules are advisory and are set in the theme; they do not stop the Shopify product feed.

questions.text: Do you want to control the answers AI assistants give about shipping, returns and sizing?
questions.help: Shopify has a free app that publishes your FAQs for assistants and logs what shoppers ask.

teach.why: Assistants answer service questions whether or not you supply the answers. Publishing them keeps the answers right and shows what customers actually ask.
teach.limits: The FAQ content is a free Shopify app; the query log shows what shoppers asked about the store.

questions.text: Do you plan to offer your own AI shopping assistant, or connect the store to agent platforms yourself?
questions.help: Parts of this are still early access at Shopify, so treat it as exploration rather than fixed scope.

native.feature: Universal Commerce Protocol and agent interfaces
native.plan_note: Universal Cart API is early access

teach.why: It separates “be present where assistants already are” from “build your own assistant”. The second is a project in its own right and partly on pre-release technology.
teach.limits: Shopify publishes an open protocol and store endpoints for agents; the cart part is early access, and plan requirements are not documented yet.

questions.text: Which Shopify AI tools do you want your team to use in day-to-day work?
questions.help: These are back-office tools for your team, not customer-facing.

native.plan_note: Included; features and limits vary by plan
Shopify or Advanced plan; under 200,000 products

teach.why: It separates customer-facing AI from staff productivity, and flags a training and governance need rather than a build.
teach.limits: The assistant and content tools are included in the plans, with limits varying by plan; better on-site search needs a specific plan and a catalogue under 200,000 products.

questions.text: Existing Shopify store: what do the agentic sales-channel settings show today (Sales channels → Agentic)?
questions.help: Check the admin with the client: enrolment mode, which channels are on, and whether checkout inside the assistant is enabled.

teach.why: On an existing store the settings are already live, so the consultant reads the current state instead of asking the client to imagine it.
teach.limits: Turning enrolment off can take up to seven days to take effect in some channels.

questions.text: List every system that exchanges product, inventory, order, customer or financial data with the store. For each: system, category, direction, data objects, frequency, connector (native app / iPaaS / custom / none), owner, status, and whether it has a test environment we can connect to before go-live.
questions.help: Typical ownership: the PIM supplies products, attributes and translations; the ERP supplies prices (including B2B catalogs), inventory per location and order status. Shopify needs no separate instance for staging, so the only environment that has to be arranged is yours: a system with no test environment means integration testing runs against your live one.

native.feature: Admin API, bulk operations and webhooks

teach.why: This table decides the integration architecture - native connector, iPaaS or custom app - and the API surface each flow needs. It is also the count behind the STOP: more than three integrations at launch is a Discovery Phase, not a build sprint.
teach.limits: Webhook delivery is not guaranteed, so a reconciliation job - a scheduled read-back or bulk query - belongs in scope for every connection, whatever the connector. The Admin API budget also differs by plan: 100 points/second on Basic and Grow, 200 on Advanced, 1000 on Plus.

questions.text: Is there a middleware / iPaaS layer, or custom connectors?

teach.why: Tells you who owns mapping, retries and error handling. An existing iPaaS turns most flows into configuration; no iPaaS and no off-the-shelf connector for the ERP or PIM flags a separate integration scoping track at T3 or T4.

options.pros: Fastest and cheapest; the vendor maintains it against Shopify's API versions
options.cons: Only covers the flows the vendor built; field mapping is often fixed; another subscription and another support boundary

options.pros: Mapping, retries, logging and monitoring already exist; the client's team can change flows without a release
options.cons: Licence and per-message cost; a second place where commerce logic lives; still needs reconciliation against Shopify

options.option: Custom app against the Admin API
options.pros: Exact control of mapping, batching and error handling; can use bulk operations for volume
options.cons: You build and keep webhook handling, retries, reconciliation and API-version upgrades; a custom app containing Functions needs Plus

questions.text: How often do prices and stock change (updates per day), and must changes be live within minutes?
questions.help: Sizes the sync design (bulk operations vs webhooks).

teach.why: Sizes the sync design and the API budget. High-volume, non-urgent updates belong in bulk operations; freshness measured in minutes means webhooks plus reconciliation. The answer also tests whether the target plan's Admin API rate limit is enough.
teach.limits: Bulk imports: the JSONL file cannot exceed 100 MB, and the operation must finish within 24 hours or it is stopped and marked failed. Admin API rate limits are per plan, so heavy sync can itself force Advanced or Plus.

questions.text: Which data must be migrated?
questions.help: Customer passwords can't be migrated; customers sign in with a one-time code.

teach.why: Shopify's own Store Migration app moves products and customers from ten named platforms. It does not move order history, reviews or prices per location. Everything outside that list is a migration app licence or a custom script, and that is where migration budgets go.
teach.limits: Passwords cannot be migrated because they are encrypted outside Shopify. Current customer accounts sign in with a one-time six-digit code, so plan the comms rather than a password migration. Products with more than three options lose their options on import; prices by location are set to the highest price.

questions.text: Approximate volumes: products, customers, orders, URL redirects.

teach.why: Volumes decide the route: CSV, a migration app, or scripted bulk imports. Redirect count matters most, because redirects are what carry the client's search traffic across - and Shopify caps them at 100,000, or 20,000,000 on Plus.
teach.limits: Customer CSV files must be 15 MB or smaller, so large bases split across several files. Products allow up to 2,048 variants, three options and 250 images. Import products first, then customers, then historical orders, so orders can connect to both.

questions.text: Must historical orders be available inside Shopify?

teach.why: The first-party migration app does not import orders. Bringing history in means a third-party importer such as Matrixify or scripted orderCreate calls - plus a rehearsal problem, because development and trial stores cap orderCreate at five orders per minute.

options.pros: Support, returns and customer lifetime value all work from one admin; no second system for staff to learn
options.cons: Not covered by the first-party app - an importer licence or a scripted build; dev-store rate caps make full-volume rehearsal impractical

options.option: Keep the old system read-only for history
options.pros: Removes the largest and riskiest part of the migration from the launch critical path
options.cons: Two places to look up an order; the legacy platform keeps costing money; reporting across the cut-over date has to be stitched together

teach.limits: Turn off new-order notifications first: every imported order emails each staff member set to receive them, including the account owner. orderCreate needs the write_orders scope and an app with an offline token.

questions.text: How much SEO equity (rankings, backlinks) must be preserved?

teach.why: Sets whether migration rides along with the build sprint or needs its own track. Shopify generates sitemap.xml automatically, but rankings survive on the redirects you author - and reindexing takes 48 to 72 hours, sometimes a few weeks.
teach.limits: Redirects are imported by CSV under Content > Menus > URL redirects, capped at 100,000 or 20,000,000 on Plus. Also remove explicit http: and https: protocols from asset URLs during the move.

questions.text: Must active subscriptions move to the new store without customers re-entering cards?

teach.why: Active subscriptions are the hardest thing to move: the contract, the stored payment credential and the billing schedule all have to survive together. If they cannot, every subscriber re-enters a card, which is a churn event rather than a task.
teach.limits: Our verified Shopify chapters document no first-party tooling for moving live subscriptions; treat it as a dedicated migration track and confirm what the current gateway and subscription app will release before committing to a date.

questions.text: Is there a Figma file or design mockup for the new store?

teach.why: Decides whether design is an input or a work package. No Figma means design effort sits inside the engagement; a complete Figma design system covering every template is an L trigger, because implementing someone else's system costs more, not less.

questions.text: How complete is it — brand only, key screens, or every template?

teach.why: Completeness is the estimate. Brand only means the theme's own sections carry the design. Key screens mean you interpolate the rest. Every template means matching each one in Liquid, which is where a theme build turns into a custom build.

questions.text: Does the Figma file contain a full design system (tokens and components)?

teach.why: Tokens and components map onto theme settings and theme blocks, which are defined at theme level and reused across sections. A file of flat screens does not, and each screen then becomes bespoke Liquid - the difference between configuring a theme and writing one.

questions.text: Is the design mapped to Shopify sections and blocks?

teach.why: A design already mapped to sections and blocks is buildable as a theme. One that is not usually hides layouts the merchant could never rebuild in the theme editor. Ask early - remapping after design sign-off is rework on both sides.
teach.limits: Sections can be added to any page of the online store except the gift card and checkout pages, so a design that assumes editable checkout layout is mapped to something that does not exist.

questions.text: Is a fully custom design required, rather than a theme with brand customisation?

teach.why: Separates brand customisation of a current-generation theme from a bespoke build. Theme architecture constrains layout; going outside it means custom sections. If the design cannot be expressed in theme architecture at all, that is a headless argument, not a styling one.

options.pros: Shortest route to launch; marketing restructures pages in the theme editor; theme app extensions install with no code
options.cons: Layout is constrained by theme architecture; a distinctive design may need custom sections anyway

options.pros: Unconstrained visual and interaction design
options.cons: Custom sections to build and maintain; every merchant-editable area has to be designed as a setting or it becomes a developer ticket

questions.text: Is a headless storefront required (Hydrogen, another framework, or a native app front end)?
questions.help: Headless means a custom front end built on Shopify; checkout stays Shopify checkout.

native.plan_note: Oxygen public environments: 1 below Plus, 25 on Plus

teach.why: The largest architectural decision in the questionnaire. The commerce engine is identical either way; what changes is who owns the presentation layer. Headless removes the theme editor, so marketing can no longer restructure pages without a release.

options.pros: Fastest to launch; merchant edits pages with sections and theme blocks; app features arrive through theme app extensions; features ship to the Online Store first
options.cons: Design constrained by theme architecture; front-end stack is Liquid

options.pros: Unconstrained design; any framework; one front end can serve more than the store
options.cons: Longest build; content editing, customer accounts, Markets, B2B, analytics and consent all have to be built; framework and security maintenance is ongoing

teach.limits: Checkout stays Shopify-hosted - you send the buyer to the cart's checkoutUrl. Customer accounts, Markets and localisation, B2B, analytics and consent each become explicit work. Oxygen public environments: 1 below Plus, 25 on Plus.

questions.text: Any theme licence to keep?
questions.help: New builds start from Shopify's Horizon theme; a third-party theme licence only matters for a non-Horizon base.

teach.why: New builds start from Shopify's Horizon theme, so an existing licence only matters if the client insists on a non-Horizon base. Inheriting a third-party theme also inherits its upgrade path and its vendor's release cadence.

questions.text: What is the aesthetic direction (minimal, editorial, luxury, playful, utilitarian)?

teach.why: Sets the theme shortlist and how much custom section work sits behind the design. Dense editorial layout, full-bleed video and heavy motion push effort into custom sections; a restrained direction is mostly theme settings and content.

questions.text: Which interactive patterns are required (mega-menu, quick-add, swatches, predictive search, lookbook, video hero)?

native.feature: Predictive search, variant swatches and filters (Search & Discovery)

teach.why: Each pattern is native, an app or a build, and the split is not obvious. Predictive search, variant swatches and filters come with Search & Discovery. Wishlists need an app. Combined listings are Plus only.
teach.limits: Combined listings: Plus. Shopify's modified storefront search needs Grow or above and fewer than 200,000 products. A wishlist app is a recurring cost and a theme integration, not a theme setting.

questions.text: Is custom motion or animation required?

teach.why: Custom motion is front-end engineering, not a theme setting, and it lands on the same Core Web Vitals the store will be judged by - Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift. Price it accordingly.

questions.text: Why headless?
questions.help: Helps check whether Horizon theme blocks would do.

teach.why: Tests the reason against the architecture. A front end serving more than the store, a design that theme architecture cannot express, or an existing CMS as source of truth are real reasons. Speed and 'modern stack' usually are not.
teach.limits: Current-generation themes with theme blocks cover far more than Online Store 2.0 did, so check the requirement against Horizon's block architecture before accepting a headless answer. A headless build also needs a standing front-end team after launch.

questions.text: Headless hosting?

teach.why: Oxygen is Shopify's serverless hosting for Hydrogen, included at no extra charge on Basic through Plus, but public environments are capped at one below Plus and 25 on Plus. Self-hosting escapes the cap and takes on the operational work.

options.pros: Included at no additional charge from Basic to Plus; edge deployment; Shopify's own Hydrogen patterns for analytics and consent
options.cons: Only one public environment below Plus, which constrains preview and staging; tied to Hydrogen; consent banner needs a custom domain

options.pros: Any framework, any number of environments, the client's existing platform and CI
options.cons: Hosting cost and operational ownership; Shopify's Hydrogen hosting patterns no longer apply out of the box

teach.limits: Oxygen is not available on the Agentic plan. Hydrogen's cookie banner does not work on default Oxygen URLs, so a custom domain is needed before consent behaves correctly.

questions.text: Where is editorial content managed for the headless storefront?

teach.why: Headless removes the theme editor, so somebody has to own content editing: whatever you build inside the storefront, or a separate CMS the client licenses and you integrate. Decide it before the build, not after launch when marketing asks.

options.pros: One system, one login, no extra licence; content sits beside the products it sells
options.cons: Editors get whatever editing experience you build; the theme editor's page-structure freedom is gone

options.pros: Purpose-built editorial tooling, workflow and multi-channel reuse; suits a brand where content leads
options.cons: Licence cost, an integration to build and maintain, and two systems that must agree on products, markets and languages

teach.limits: A CMS is a licence, an integration and a second publishing workflow, and it adds a preview and cache story on the storefront side.

questions.text: Which front end: Shopify Hydrogen, or another framework?

teach.why: This is the line between a Shopify engagement and a composable one. Hydrogen is Shopify’s own framework on the Storefront API, and with content in metaobjects it is still a Shopify build. Another framework, a native app, or several front ends on one backend is Merkle Arc, and these offers do not price it.
teach.limits: Hydrogen needs the Storefront API on any plan, and Oxygen is included from Basic upward. Below Plus only one Oxygen environment can be public, so parallel stakeholder review links need a store login.

options.pros: Stays inside the offers, and inside Shopify: one system, the Storefront API, Oxygen hosting included, and content in metaobjects beside the products it sells.
options.cons: React and a deployment pipeline to own; the theme editor is gone, so editors get whatever editing experience is built for them.

options.option: Another framework, a native app, or several front ends
options.pros: Whatever the brand already runs on, and one backend behind several experiences.
options.cons: Not a Shopify build: it goes to Merkle Arc, which scopes and prices it separately. Nothing in these offers estimates it.

questions.text: Headless platform features required?

native.plan_note: Cookie banner does not work on default Oxygen URLs

teach.why: Each feature named here is work the Online Store gives you for nothing. Customer accounts mean OAuth against the Customer Account API; Markets means querying international prices and setting cart context yourself; analytics and consent follow Hydrogen's patterns or are built from scratch.
teach.limits: B2B works only with customer accounts, and buyer-specific routes cannot be cached because the queries return personalised data. Hydrogen's cookie banner does not work on default Oxygen URLs.

questions.text: Do you want to A/B test themes or checkout configurations?
questions.help: Native with Shopify Rollouts experiments.

teach.why: Native theme and checkout experiments run on Shopify Rollouts, and Rollouts starts at the Grow plan. A Basic client who expects to A/B test is therefore a plan conversation or a third-party app - and it surfaces late unless you ask now.
teach.limits: Rollouts experiments: Grow plan and above.

questions.text: Do you want a presence inside Shopify’s Shop app — a Shop Mini?
questions.help: A full-screen shopping experience inside the Shop app. It is not your own app and not a headless storefront.

teach.why: Wanting to be on a phone does not mean building an app. A Shop Mini reaches Shop’s buyers without a storefront of your own and without leaving Shopify; a standalone native app is the Storefront API plus Checkout Kit, which is a headless build and a different engagement.
teach.limits: A Mini "must function solely within the Shop app; it cannot be a standalone app that operates outside of the Shop." It is built with the Shop Minis React SDK, so it is React Native work rather than theme work.

options.pros: Reaches Shop’s buyers, stays inside Shopify, and the commerce engine is the store you already have.
options.cons: Lives only inside Shop — no icon on a home screen and no presence outside that app.

options.pros: Your brand on the home screen, your notifications, your rules.
options.cons: Storefront API plus Checkout Kit: a headless build, which leaves these offers and is scoped by Merkle Arc.

questions.text: Which accessibility standard applies?
questions.help: Shopify checkout is tested against WCAG 2.2 AA; the theme and apps are your responsibility (e.g. under the European Accessibility Act).

teach.why: Shopify's checkout is tested against WCAG 2.2 AA, but the theme, the apps and any headless front end are the client's responsibility. Under the European Accessibility Act that is legal exposure, not a quality preference - and it decides QA scope.

questions.text: Has an accessibility audit been done on the current site?

teach.why: An existing audit turns accessibility from an unknown into a defect list you can size. No audit, on a site heading for a legal deadline, means remediation scope is open-ended - put the audit in the plan rather than discovering it at UAT.

questions.text: Core Web Vitals targets: LCP (seconds), CLS, INP (milliseconds).

teach.why: Numbers make performance testable rather than arguable. Shopify reports the same three Core Web Vitals - Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift - so targets in those units can be verified in the admin after launch.
teach.limits: The web performance report covers the Online Store; a headless storefront needs its own monitoring, and its performance depends on the code and hosting you choose. Data covers the last 90 days and can lag by up to 36 hours.

questions.text: Is page speed a known problem today?
questions.help: Shopify's web performance report shows Core Web Vitals for the current store.

teach.why: If the current store is already on Shopify, its web performance report is evidence rather than opinion: the three Core Web Vitals, on real traffic. If the store is elsewhere, treat the answer as a hypothesis until you measure it.
teach.limits: The report holds only the last 90 days and can be delayed by up to 36 hours, so a recent change may not show yet.

questions.text: Which third-party scripts must load (chat, personalisation, heatmaps)?

teach.why: Third-party scripts are the usual reason a Shopify storefront is slow, and they arrive after you leave - chat, personalisation, heatmaps, tag managers. Listing them now lets you set a budget and decide what loads on which template before targets are agreed.
teach.limits: Scripts affect the same Core Web Vitals the client will measure you against, and each one is a consent and data-protection question as well as a performance one.

questions.text: What is the target go-live date?
questions.help: A date sooner than the delivery time the scope needs leads to a phased, MVP-first plan.

teach.why: The go-live date sets the whole plan. Exit rule 11.15 compares the weeks from kick-off to go-live against the offer's minimum duration; if the date is too soon, the engagement is re-scoped MVP-first before any sprint begins.
teach.limits: Rule 11.15 counts from delivery.kickoff_date, falling back to the date discovery was created, so an unknown kick-off makes the check optimistic.

questions.text: What drives the deadline (peak season, product launch, contract end)?

teach.why: A deadline fixed by something outside the project — peak season, a collection launch, a contract end — cannot move. That changes the risk register: scope absorbs any slippage, not the date. A soft internal target leaves you room to negotiate.

questions.text: Is a phased launch planned?

teach.why: Tells you whether you are planning one launch or several. A phased launch lets the first release stay narrow and pushes the risky parts back; a single launch means everything must be ready on the day.

options.pros: Earlier go-live on a narrow scope; risky work moves to a later phase; real traffic informs what comes next.
options.cons: More releases to plan, test and support, and the client lives with known gaps for a while.

options.pros: One cutover, one communications moment, nothing half-finished on the storefront.
options.cons: Everything must be ready on the date; any slip moves the entire launch.

questions.text: Preferred project kick-off date.

teach.why: Kick-off starts the clock used by exit rule 11.15 — the available weeks are counted from here. A late kick-off against a fixed go-live shortens delivery without shortening scope, and you want that visible in discovery, not in sprint two.

questions.text: Who is involved on the client side? For each: role, RACI (R/A/C/I), decision-maker (yes/no). Names are optional.

teach.why: The RACI map tells you who approves, who must be consulted and who only needs telling. Every 'C' adds a feedback loop to each design, content and scope review, and approvers nobody named surface later as delay.

questions.text: Is there a single decision-maker for scope, approvals and feedback?
questions.help: A single decision-maker must be named before the statement of work.

teach.why: Exit rule 11.16 flags this. Without one named decision-maker, scope questions get several answers and approvals stall — the commonest cause of overrun. The name must be confirmed before the statement of work is signed.
teach.limits: Rule 11.16 is a FLAG, not a STOP: discovery continues, but the flag must be cleared before signature.

questions.text: Is budget approval authority clear?

teach.why: The same exit rule 11.16. If nobody can say yes to money, the scope you agree is provisional — change requests, apps with monthly fees and the retainer all stall. Name the budget owner before the statement of work.
teach.limits: Rule 11.16 is a FLAG, not a STOP: discovery continues, but the budget owner must be confirmed before signature.

questions.text: Which training is needed (products, orders, discounts, reports)?

teach.why: This decides how much handover you build and price. Training on products, orders, discounts and reports is real delivery work — sessions, materials, recordings. Anything not listed here is outside scope and returns later as support tickets.

questions.text: Are written SOPs required?

teach.why: Written standard operating procedures are a deliverable in their own right: someone drafts, reviews and maintains them. Asking now stops them appearing as an unplanned request in the final sprint.

options.pros: The client's team can run the store unaided; fewer support tickets and less key-person risk.
options.cons: Drafting, reviewing and maintaining them is effort that must be scoped and priced.

options.pros: Lighter handover; live training and recordings may be enough for a small team.
options.cons: Knowledge stays with individuals, and every change becomes a question for the retainer.

questions.text: What post-launch support model is expected?

teach.why: This shapes everything after go-live: who fixes a broken checkout at the weekend, who loads next season's collection. The expected model drives the retainer conversation and decides what team stays in place after launch.

options.pros: Named team, agreed response times and planned improvements after go-live.
options.cons: A recurring commitment the client must budget and approve.

options.pros: The client pays only when something is actually needed.
options.cons: No guaranteed availability; urgent fixes compete with other work and cost more.

options.pros: Lowest ongoing cost and fastest internal turnaround for routine changes.
options.cons: Requires full training and SOPs at handover, which enlarges the delivery scope.

questions.text: Is the Grow retainer signed?

teach.why: Exit rule 11.11 warns when an M or L engagement has no signed Grow retainer. The build is priced assuming work continues after launch; without the signature the commercials are adjusted. Check the signature, not the intention.
teach.limits: Rule 11.11 is a WARN and applies to M and L engagements only; it does not stop discovery.

questions.text: Retainer length in months.

teach.why: The length decides how long the team stays and how much post-launch work is already covered. It feeds the commercial model and tells the client exactly what they get after go-live instead of leaving it open.

questions.text: Will the client re-verify apps and Shopify features at each Shopify Edition after launch?

teach.why: Shopify announces platform changes at each Edition, and the apps and features the store depends on can change. Someone has to re-verify them. A no here means nobody is watching the store drift — which usually becomes retainer work.

questions.text: Is the business in a regulated industry (pharma, alcohol, firearms, age-restricted goods, financial products, medical devices)? If yes, which?
questions.help: A regulated industry needs legal review. Shopify has its own rules: e.g. alcohol needs age verification; some business types can't use Shopify Payments.

native.feature: Shopify rules for regulated goods (e.g. alcohol)

teach.why: This is a STOP. Exit rule 11.8 sends any regulated business — pharma, alcohol, firearms, age-restricted goods, financial products, medical devices — to legal and compliance review. Shopify has its own rules too, and some business types cannot use Shopify Payments.
teach.limits: Shopify's rules for regulated goods (alcohol, for example) apply from the Basic plan; age-verification apps are on the shortlist. Verified 2026-09-17.

questions.text: Are legal pages (terms, privacy, cookies, returns) ready, in need of updates, or still to be drafted?

teach.why: Legal pages are content somebody must write, approve and publish before launch. 'Still to be drafted' is a client task on the critical path, usually with a lawyer in the loop — not a theme job you can finish in a sprint.

questions.text: Any other industry-specific compliance requirements?

teach.why: This catches the requirement nobody thought to mention — licensing, labelling, record-keeping, industry codes. It is the safety net for exit rule 11.8: anything raised here goes to the same legal review before scope is fixed.

questions.text: Is the business and product range eligible for Shopify Payments (no restricted or prohibited categories)?

teach.why: Shopify Payments is not open to every country or every business category. If the client is not eligible, the payment stack, the fees and part of the checkout experience change, so this must be settled in discovery, not at launch.
teach.limits: Eligibility depends on the store's country and on the product categories sold; the supported-countries page is the reference. Verified 2026-09-17.

questions.text: Lead consultant.

teach.why: The named consultant owns the engagement record. Every artefact the tool produces — engagement file, deck, backlog, closing document — carries this name, so each answer and judgement can be traced back to a person.

questions.text: Has the client agreed that their answers may be processed by AI (no customer personal data included)?
questions.help: Nothing else can be recorded until this is Yes, and it has to be true — an RFP arriving in your inbox is not consent to put it through an AI tool. If the client’s process has no such clause, ask, or stop.

teach.why: Under ADR 0007 the engine refuses to run without recorded consent. Nothing is processed, stored or generated until the client has agreed to AI processing. Record it explicitly, and keep customer personal data out of the answers regardless.
teach.limits: Consent covers the discovery answers only; customer personal data must never be entered, with or without consent.

questions.text: Jira site and project key for the backlog.

teach.why: The backlog is generated for import into the client's Jira. The site and project key tell the tool where the tickets belong; without them the export is generic and somebody re-keys it by hand.

questions.text: Jira components to use.

teach.why: Components let the generated tickets land inside the client's existing Jira structure rather than as a flat list. It is the difference between a backlog the delivery team can use on day one and one somebody has to sort first.

questions.text: The requirements go beyond the S, M and L offers. How will Merkle proceed: a Larger Engagement, or Merkle Arc?
questions.help: Larger Engagement: Merkle proposes an Enterprise Engagement with a dedicated Discovery Phase; the approach, a brief and the client deck are still produced, Jira tickets are not. Merkle Arc: the storefront is not a Shopify theme, so the Arc practice scopes and prices it as a separate engagement — the discovery and the approach go across with it, and nothing here quotes or estimates it. Deciding not to bid is recorded on the outcome ledger instead, once the decision is actually taken.

teach.why: After a STOP the engagement cannot continue as a standard offer, and the tool must know which output to produce. Larger Engagement drafts the approach, brief and client deck with no Jira tickets. Merkle Arc hands the storefront build to the Arc practice with the discovery behind it; this engine prices Shopify builds and does not price Arc.

options.pros: Keeps the client; the blocker gets a dedicated Discovery Phase with the right people and budget.
options.cons: Longer sales cycle, no Jira tickets and no delivery start now; needs a Merkle Enterprise Engagement to be viable.

options.pros: Keeps the work inside Merkle, where a tokenised design system and a component library already exist. The commerce engine can still be Shopify.
options.cons: A different practice, a different rate card and a different timeline. The S, M and L bands do not apply and nothing here estimates it.

questions.text: Where will customer questions be answered after launch: Shopify Inbox, a helpdesk app, a helpdesk outside Shopify, email only, or nowhere yet?
questions.help: Shopify Inbox is free and lives in the admin. A helpdesk such as Gorgias or Zendesk pulls order context in and usually needs a connection built.

teach.why: Where a question lands decides whether anything has to be integrated at all. A helpdesk outside Shopify needs order and customer context sent to it, which is an integration with a cost; Shopify Inbox needs none.
teach.limits: A helpdesk outside Shopify counts as an integration only when the connector is custom-built — an App Store app with a native connector is an app.

questions.text: Which helpdesk, if one is named?
questions.help: The product name, not a person.

teach.why: Named early, it can be checked against the App Store registry for a native connector before anyone assumes a custom build.

questions.text: Where should the storefront contact form deliver: an email inbox, the helpdesk, a CRM, or is there no form?
questions.help: Shopify themes ship a contact form that sends email. Anything else is a connection somebody builds and maintains.

teach.why: The theme contact form sends email and nothing else. If it has to open a case or create a CRM record, that is build work and it is routinely assumed rather than scoped.

questions.text: Does your team create orders for customers — by phone, in a showroom, or for wholesale buyers?
questions.help: In Shopify this is a draft order: staff build the order in the admin and send an invoice to pay.

teach.why: Ordering on behalf of a customer is a real workflow with permissions, payment and tax consequences, and it is invisible on the storefront. Unasked, it arrives after launch as a change request.
teach.limits: Draft orders are created in the admin or through the API; the customer pays by invoice link. Staff need the right permission, and the order still has to pick up the correct market prices and tax.

questions.text: Do customers book a slot with you — an in-store appointment, a virtual consultation, or both?
questions.help: Booking is not a Shopify feature; it is an App Store category, and the app is what holds the calendar.

teach.why: A boutique appointment or a fitting is a real part of how some brands sell, and Shopify has nothing native for it — so it is an app with a licence, a calendar owner and a place in the staff’s day, decided on the ladder like any other app rather than assumed into the theme.
teach.limits: No native Shopify booking feature: appointments and services are an App Store category. Multi-location scheduling, staff portals, deposits and reminders differ by app, so the shortlist is made against what this client actually needs.
